sources.news_title: Trump targets green card path used by Microsoft and other Tech firms
sources.text:
Why Trump is targeting green card path used by Microsoft, other tech firms
- Trump has suspended PERM green card sponsorship for Microsoft and other tech firms, saying the system is abused and should protect US workers more.
- PERM lets employers seek permanent residency for foreign staff after wage checks and 60 days of job adverts, but delays and backlogs are common.
- The administration is also tightening H-1B rules and plans a PERM overhaul, while companies face pressure to train and hire more American workers.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - From the start of his second term, US President Donald Trump has made it a top priority to restrict opportunities for non-Americans to gain entry or remain in the United States. In the latest action on that front, his administration said on Oct 8 that it would indefinitely suspend the ability of a number of technology companies, including Microsoft Corp, to sponsor foreign employees for permanent residency in the US.
Such companies have been relatively heavy users of the government’s Permanent Labor Certification process, a step in the path towards a green card, which confers permanent residency. The administration alleges there have been widespread abuses of the programme. Earlier in 2026, the administration took steps to overhaul the H-1B visa programme, arguing it also has been exploited by employers.
What’s the Permanent Labor Certification process?
The process, known as PERM, is a government system for vetting applications by employers who want to secure green cards for foreign workers. Typically, employers file applications on behalf of foreign employees who are already working for them in the US on a temporary basis.
First, an employer is required to have the Department of Labor determine a minimum wage for the relevant position based on the job duties and geographic market. After that, the employer must advertise the job for 60 days to test whether there are qualified American workers interested in applying. When the recruitment period concludes, the employer can submit an application for permanent labour certification, which can take well over a year to clear because of large processing backlogs.
The Labor Department is required to consider whether there are Americans “willing, qualified and available” to do the same work and whether the employment of the foreigner will negatively affect the wages and working conditions of comparable US workers.
In fiscal 2025, it approved some 138,000 applications. Another 3,400 were denied and 6,700 withdrawn.
The approvals cover a wide range of occupations. The top eight are software developers; computer systems analysts; meat, poultry and fish cutters and trimmers; data scientists; fast food and counter workers; project management specialists; software analysts; and landscapers and groundskeepers.
How is PERM different from the H-1B programme?
H-1Bs, which are temporary work visas, are the primary pathway to hire foreign workers with at least a college degree for specialised occupations. The maximum time a worker can stay in the US on an H-1B visa is generally six years. If an employer wants to retain the worker long term in the US, it can apply for a permanent labour certification. In that case, the H-1B can be extended continuously if at least a year has passed since the employer filed for the certification. The biggest PERM filers have historically been the largest employers of H-1B workers.
Arguing that employers have used the H-1B programme to displace American workers, the Trump administration earlier in 2026 revamped an annual lottery for 85,000 visa slots to favour the most highly paid workers. It has also announced a US$100,000 (S$128,000) fee for new H-1B workers hired from outside the US, but courts have blocked the imposition of it.
How important is PERM to the tech industry?
A large proportion of PERM applications are for positions in the tech industry. In 2025, almost a third of all approved applications were for software and computer systems analysis roles. Microsoft was the top PERM filer in fiscal 2025. Green card sponsorship, which begins with a PERM filing, is an important recruitment and retention tool of employers competing for high-skilled foreign talent.
Why is the programme under scrutiny from the Trump administration?
The Trump administration has been sharply critical of Silicon Valley’s reliance on foreign workers and has pressured tech giants to do more to train and hire US workers. In announcing the suspension, Vice-President J.D. Vance did not specify alleged abuses but accused Microsoft and other companies of “importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do”.
In addition to Microsoft, the administration has suspended use of the PERM process for staffing firms Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp, Infosys Ltd, Tata, Wipro Ltd, HCL Technologies Ltd and Capgemini SE.
This is not the first time the administration has brought enforcement actions against US companies on the basis of alleged abuse of PERM. A unit of OpenAI reached a US$3.2 million settlement in August with the Justice Department to resolve allegations of discrimination against US workers. And the Labor Department took the rare step earlier in 2026 of suspending PERM applications by software firm Cloudera Inc over recruitment violations.
Justice Department investigations launched during Trump’s first term into alleged PERM recruitment violations by Apple Inc. and Meta led to large settlements.
What changes are planned for PERM?
The Trump administration plans to overhaul the regulations governing the PERM process, which were last updated more than two decades ago. A Labor Department rule currently under review at the White House would modernize how the agency reviews applications and bring a new emphasis to protecting American workers, the administration has said. sources.news_title: Trump Administration Suspends Microsoft, Adobe, and a Half-Dozen IT Outsourcers from Green Card Program
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said Thursday the Labor Department is suspending Microsoft, Adobe and six of the largest IT outsourcing firms from the Permanent Labor Certification Program, the step most employers must clear before sponsoring a foreign worker for a green card.
Sonderling made the announcement at a White House press conference on visa fraud, with Vance standing beside him. “I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world — Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini — and also, due to multiple active federal investigations, the Department of Labor is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the program,” he said, in remarks posted by the White House rapid-response account.
“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said. He said that since 2009 the named companies had requested almost 3 million foreign workers, received more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and more than 100,000 permanent labor certifications. “That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” he said. “The Department of Labor is taking historic action by shutting down the pipeline of systemic fraud.”
Vance singled out Microsoft. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” he said. He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while receiving about 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replace that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” he said. The White House account put the PERM figure at 3,682 applications, including nearly 1,000 for the same positions as the laid-off American workers.
“Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said. He said the administration would keep working with the company but would “deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.”
The Permanent Labor Certification process, known as PERM, is run by the Labor Department. Before most employment-based green cards can move forward, an employer has to show that no able-bodied, willing, and qualified U.S. worker is available for the job and that hiring the foreign worker will not hurt the wages or working conditions of U.S. workers. A certification is not itself a green card. It is the labor-market test that comes first.
The six outsourcers are the firms that staff U.S. companies with workers brought in on temporary visas, then often move those workers toward permanent residency. Cognizant is a Teaneck, New Jersey, IT services company. Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies are based in India. Capgemini is based in France. Microsoft and Adobe, both U.S. software companies, were suspended separately, Sonderling said, because of active federal investigations.
Microsoft pushed back. In a statement provided by spokeswoman Kaitlin Haskins, the company told Reuters it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category” and that it builds its workforce by “strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world.” Microsoft said about 80 percent of its H-1B filings in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of people already on staff, not to hire new workers, and that the remaining filings for new employees were for people already legally in the United States and equaled about 1 percent of its U.S. workforce. It said H-1B employees are paid the same as other employees doing comparable work. Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment, Reuters reported.
Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated over what the administration called misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages. Labor Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas had already been served, Reuters reported. The university probes are separate from the company suspensions.
The announcement follows the administration’s Project Firewall effort and a White House proclamation that put a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad. Reuters reported that Project Firewall has opened about 200 cases and assessed millions of dollars in penalties. The PERM suspension does not, by itself, cancel existing H-1B visas; however it does stop the named companies from using the labor certification that is the usual on-ramp from a temporary work visa to a green card.
– – –
Christina Botteri is the Executive Editor of The Tennessee Star and The Star News Network. Follow her on X at @christinakb.

sources.news_title: Explainer-The skilled foreign tech workers’ green card program under attack from Trump - Regional Media News
sources.text:
By Deborah Mary Sophia and Jaspreet Singh
Oct 8 (Reuters) – The US government said on Thursday it is suspending some of the world’s biggest tech and IT firms including Microsoft, Cognizant and Capgemini from a key green card program that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency through their employment.
Senior US officials cited alleged fraud as the reason behind the move, saying companies have been using the program to replace American workers with cheaper foreign workers, and comes as the latest step in the Trump administration’s crackdown on skilled foreign labor.
WHAT IS UNDER SUSPENSION?
The suspension is targeting a key employer-sponsorship mechanism, called the Permanent Labor Certification or PERM, which is used by major technology companies and outsourcing firms. The US government said that for certain companies, it would not accept any new PERM applications or process any pending ones.
PERM came into effect in 2005, aiming to speed up the long processing times experienced under the previous paper-based “Alien Employment Certification” program.
Under the program, the US Department of Labor (DOL) allows an employer to sponsor a foreign worker permanent residency. The process is initiated by qualified US employers, and not individual workers.
The Labor Department must certify to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services that there are not enough US workers that are qualified and available for a given job opportunity, and that the employment of the foreign worker will not affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed Americans.
Outside of PERM and family-based routes to permanent residency, individuals can also self-petition for green cards through processes such as the EB-1A application for individuals with extraordinary ability or the EB-2 National Interest Waiver.
WHY IS IT IMPORTANT?
The PERM program serves as a critical bridge between temporary work status and a green card for many foreign skilled workers. Many IT firms employ hundreds of thousands of workers who typically start on temporary work visas such as the H-1B, and later seek permanent residency.
Without the option to be sponsored by their employer under PERM, foreign workers could lose a key route to permanent residency and would have to stay on temporary visas for longer. For companies, recruiting foreign talent could become harder, as many workers overseas view the path to permanent US residency as a key reason for taking a job.
WHICH COMPANIES ARE UNDER SUSPENSION?
The US said it is suspending Microsoft and Adobe along with some of the largest IT firms in the world, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.
Other companies such as Meta, Amazon or Alphabet’s Google remain free to participate in the program.
WHY IS THE US FREEZING APPLICATIONS?
The move widens an ongoing crackdown on visas which the Trump administration has said cost US jobs. Vice President JD Vance said, without citing specific evidence, companies are using the PERM program to replace American employees with foreign workers and undercut their wages.
Vance said on Thursday: “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”
The suspensions follow President Trump’s move to impose a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions for highly skilled foreign workers, which has been blocked by federal court orders.
HOW IS PERM DIFFERENT FROM H-1B?
H-1B is a temporary work visa that allows skilled foreign workers to work in the US, generally for up to six years. PERM meanwhile is a permanent labor-certification process. The freeze does not appear to directly affect current holders of H-1B visas.
HOW CURTAILING PERM COULD BACKFIRE
Some experts said that while the PERM suspensions might target specific companies, such policies risk making the US less competitive globally by deterring highly skilled foreign talent.
“It is a fallacy to think that you can protect American workers by keeping skilled foreign workers out of the country. You think that foreign talent competes with Americans within our borders, they’ll certainly compete with Americans by working abroad,” said Chad Sparber, Director of the Lampert Institute for Civic and Global Affairs at Colgate University.
Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford’s Immigration Policy Lab, said that permanent residency is the primary way for talented foreign workers to stay in the country and without it, some will leave, and some will not come in the first place, even temporarily.
(Reporting by Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru; Editing by Christian Plumb)

Vice President JD Vance announced that the Trump administration has suspended numerous technology firms, including Microsoft, from the Program Electronic Review Management (PERM) Program.

sources.news_title: US freezes Microsoft, Adobe visas over alleged fraud
sources.text:
US freezes Microsoft, Adobe visas over alleged fraud
US President Donald Trump's administration has frozen some green-card filings by Microsoft, Adobe and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine elite universities, widening a visa crackdown it says targets fraud and local job losses.
The twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs, potentially blocking a common path to permanent residency for thousands of foreign tech workers while putting some of the country's most prominent research universities on notice.
"Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers," Vice President JD Vance said.
US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.
"We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said.
Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages.
Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment.
Under the Labor Department's permanent labour certification process, known as PERM, which is required for most employment-based green cards, employers must show that hiring a foreign worker will not harm the wages, working conditions or job opportunities of US workers. Approved applications then go to US Citizenship and Immigration Services.
The freeze does not appear to directly affect current holders of H-1B visas, which allow companies to employ foreign workers temporarily. But it could block a common route by which employers sponsor those workers for permanent residency.
Indian IT firms such as Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL, along with Cognizant, have long been among the biggest users of H-1B visas.
Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to USCIS data.
Microsoft is also the largest filer of PERM applications, according to Permtrack.app, which compiles Labor Department disclosure data.
The suspensions are the latest in a series of steps against skilled-worker programs. In September last year, the Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called Project Firewall, as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time $US100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad.
During President Donald Trump's second term, companies have faced growing pressure to keep jobs and production in the United States rather than move them overseas.
The action comes despite closer ties between the administration and tech leaders, who are lobbying for lighter AI regulation. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella was among the executives at a White House AI summit on September 29.
The nine universities also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Vance accused them of using J-1 exchange-visitor visas to bring in international students and undercut American wages. Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.
with AP

sources.news_title: Vance Freezes Microsoft’s Green-Card Pipeline, Demands American Workers Come First – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Jack
sources.text:
JD Vance just put one of America’s biggest technology companies on notice: being successful does not earn you a free pass on American jobs.
The Trump administration announced Thursday that Microsoft is being suspended from the federal labor-certification program companies use to sponsor workers for employment-based green cards.
Adobe and six major IT outsourcing firms are also caught in the crackdown.
This is a concrete restriction on the companies’ access to the immigration system, and Vance made clear that he wants a change in hiring practices.
Watch his announcement:
Vice President JD Vance announces the suspension of the PERM Program for Microsoft:
"Thanks to an ongoing investigation, we have decided to suspend the PERM program for Microsoft, which means they will no longer be able to take those H-1Bs and apply for permanent resident status… pic.twitter.com/xMSgLgcqTI
— Vice President JD Vance (@VP) October 8, 2026
The administration puts American workers at the center
As RealClearPolitics reports, Vance connected the suspension to an ongoing investigation and accused companies of making improper representations when seeking access to foreign-worker programs.
Pressed by a reporter to explain the alleged fraud, he argued that businesses cannot legitimately claim they need specialized foreign talent while using the system to replace Americans and drive down wages.
He also said the administration wants the technology industry to succeed and keep investing in the United States. His demand is that American workers benefit from that success, rather than being treated as an expense to eliminate.
That is an important distinction for a company with Microsoft’s influence: support for American technology does not have to mean accepting every hiring practice without scrutiny.
A famous logo should not buy a company an exemption from the rules everyone else has to follow.
Vance cited Microsoft’s layoffs and visa figures in laying out his accusation. Microsoft has since disputed the implication that its applications represented thousands of new foreign hires; its response is below.
BREAKING: VP JD Vance takes aim at Microsoft, accusing the tech giant of laying off thousands of American workers while bringing in foreign workers to replace them through the H-1B visa system.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the… pic.twitter.com/qucLP6IfbT
— Fox News (@FoxNews) October 8, 2026
Eight companies, and a freeze on pending applications
The Lynnwood Times reports that the suspension covers Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department would stop accepting new permanent labor-certification applications from the named companies and stop processing their pending applications. He cited active federal investigations in announcing the action against Microsoft and Adobe.
For businesses that rely on sponsoring workers for permanent residency, that reaches beyond future recruiting plans. It puts an immediate obstacle in front of applications already moving through the system.
The freeze concerns the labor-certification process; it does not automatically cancel existing H-1B visas or mean that every foreign employee at these companies must leave the country. Keeping those distinctions straight matters when an announcement affects real employees and their families.
Here is Sonderling identifying the companies and explaining the action:
.@Sonderling47: "I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world — Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini — and also, due to multiple active federal investigations, @USDOL is suspending… https://t.co/ENyAFHSo93 pic.twitter.com/DZXcRMp22L
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 8, 2026
What this program is supposed to do
The Department of Labor explains that permanent labor certification, commonly called PERM, is a step most employers must complete before submitting an employment-based immigration petition to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
Labor must determine that enough qualified, willing and available U.S. workers cannot be found for the particular job in the relevant area. It must also determine that hiring the foreign worker will not harm the wages and working conditions of comparable American workers.
In plain English, protecting American workers is already part of the program’s purpose. It is not an extra condition Vance invented at a press conference.
That is why the hiring records matter so much here: the central question is whether the companies met those requirements in the actual jobs and applications under review.
Americans who have lost work deserve more than a corporate slogan about talent shortages. They deserve to know whether they received a genuine chance at the jobs in question.
Microsoft pushes back on the numbers
In its Thursday statement, Microsoft said about 80% of the approximately 6,000 H-1B applications it submitted in the last fiscal year involved extending or changing the status of people it already employed.
The company said the remaining applications for new employees concerned people already legally in the United States, and that those hires equaled about 1% of its U.S. workforce. It also said most of its U.S. employees are Americans.
Microsoft defended its compensation practices, saying H-1B workers receive the same pay as other employees doing comparable work. It said it looks forward to giving the administration additional information.
That response makes a meaningful point about how to read the totals: a visa application is not automatically a new arrival or a one-for-one replacement for a laid-off worker.
It does not, by itself, resolve whether particular labor-certification applications complied with the rules. That requires the underlying records, not competing press statements.
The suspension is real; allegations of fraud still need to be established. Readers should not confuse an announced investigation with a court finding that every company on the list broke the law.
Now comes the test
The administration has put a meaningful tool behind its America First message. The next test is whether investigators can document the alleged abuses and whether the companies change any practices the evidence shows were improper.
Microsoft says its records will tell a different story. Fine: produce them and let the investigation establish what happened.
American workers deserve an immigration system that keeps its promises to them. Even when the company asking for access is Microsoft.

sources.news_title: JD Vance Makes Announcement Suspending Several Tech Firms, Including Microsoft and Adobe, from H1B Visa Program

During the press conference, JD Vance announced that Microsoft and Adobe have been suspended from the H1B visa process, as well as several other tech companies. The taskforce also announced immediate investigations into nine major U.S. universities for J1 student visa fraud. The entire visa program is being targeted by the fraud taskforce and DOJ in order to ensure that American students and American workers benefit from employment and college entrance opportunities. This is well worth watching in full:

So after a couple of cycles of H-1B reapplication, the companies will then apply for a perm, a PERM, which will allow the employee to stay, get a green card, and potentially stay in the United States indefinitely. So if the H-1B visa is how people come into the country, the perm. Program is how they stay in the United States to begin with.
Now, there has been no company in the United States unfortunately that has abused this system more than Microsoft. And let me just give you a couple of statistics on this. So in the last year, Microsoft, and I want to be clear about the data here, so let me check this, but Microsoft laid off last year 6000, 6000 American workers. At the same time, the company benefited from 6300 H-1B visas and almost 3000 green cards.

Congress capped the number of new H-1B visas issued each fiscal year (65,000 regular-cap slots plus 20,000 under the master’s-degree exemption), which is why USCIS runs a registration lottery when demand exceeds supply.

Institutions of higher education — accredited colleges and universities as defined by the Higher Education Act.Nonprofit entities related to or affiliated with an institution of higher education — this is the category that causes the most confusion, covered in detail below.Nonprofit research organizations — nonprofits whose primary mission is research, even without a university tie.Governmental research organizations — research arms of federal, state, or local government.

Microsoft Hit by Green Card Freeze as JD Vance Accuses It of Replacing US Workers With Foreign Hires
Microsoft and seven other firms face halt to new and pending PERM applications amid alleged visa abuse crackdown
Microsoft has been suspended from a US labour-certification pathway used in the employment-based green-card process after Vice President JD Vance accused the technology giant of replacing American workers with foreign hires.
The Trump administration announced the action on 8 October, suspending Microsoft and seven other companies from the Permanent Labor Certification programme, known as PERM. Vance said Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 US workers while obtaining 6,300 H-1B visas.
Vance Links Microsoft Layoffs to Foreign Hires
The H-1B programme allows employers to hire foreign workers temporarily for speciality occupations. PERM is a separate Department of Labor process generally used by employers seeking to sponsor eligible foreign workers for permanent residency.
'There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,' Vance said, according to CNN.
He also alleged that Microsoft had replaced each laid-off worker with one and a half 'foreign indentured servants'.
The numerical comparison does not, by itself, establish that the foreign workers replaced the employees who were laid off. H-1B filings can include extensions or changes of status for existing employees rather than applications for newly hired workers.
Microsoft Says Most Applications Concerned Existing Employees
In a statement published on 8 October, Microsoft said about 80% of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications it submitted in the previous fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees, rather than hire new people.
The company said the remaining filings concerned new employees already legally in the United States and represented only 1% of its US workforce. It also said its H-1B employees received the same pay as other employees doing comparable work.
Microsoft said the vast majority of its employees in the United States were Americans and that it looked forward to providing the administration with further information.
The statement set out the company's position on its immigration filings. Its figures were not independently verified for this article.
Eight Companies Suspended From PERM
US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the Department of Labor would neither accept new applications nor process pending permanent labour-certification applications involving Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.
Microsoft and Adobe are technology companies, while the other six provide IT and technology services.
Officials cited alleged fraud in announcing the suspensions. The action does not, by itself, establish that the companies committed wrongdoing.
The administration did not announce an end date. Vance said the restrictions would remain in place 'as long as it needs to'.
The suspension concerns the labour-certification stage of green-card sponsorship, rather than a cancellation of existing H-1B visas. It prevents new and pending PERM applications involving the affected companies from moving forward.
Announcement Came Before Nadella Award Ceremony
The announcement came hours before President Donald Trump presented Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
The medal is the US government's highest honour for technological achievement. The ceremony took place later on the same day that the administration announced the PERM suspension and accused Microsoft of abusing the immigration system.
Nine Universities Face J-1 Visa Probe
The administration separately announced investigations into nine universities over alleged misuse of the J-1 exchange visitor programme, which allows foreign nationals to participate in approved educational and cultural exchange programmes.
The institutions are Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, the University of California, Davis, the California Institute of Technology, Arizona State University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.
'We will investigate whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research,' he said.
Vance accused the universities of using J-1 visa holders to undercut the wages of American graduate students and researchers. Those allegations remain the subject of the announced investigations, rather than established findings of wrongdoing.
The university investigations concern the J-1 programme and are separate from the PERM suspensions imposed on Microsoft and the seven other companies.

sources.news_title: Trump Administration Cuts Off Access to a Major Immigration Program for Workers at Microsoft and Adobe
sources.text:
The Trump administration will no longer allow Microsoft and other tech companies to participate in a program that allows H-1B visa holders to apply for green cards, one of the most common pathways for skilled foreign workers seeking permanent residency in the United States.
In addition to Microsoft, administration officials said on Thursday that software giant Adobe and IT companies including Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata will be suspended from the PERM program, the Labor Department's permanent labor certification program. PERM is a key step for H-1B visa holders to gain permanent residency, requiring employers to prove that there are no American workers who would be suitable for the applicant's permanent job opportunity.
Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said that the agency is investigating whether these companies committed fraud, undercutting American workers by hiring foreign employees.
Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, singled out Microsoft. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said during a press conference.
In a statement provided by Microsoft representative Kaitlin Haskins, the company said it “only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," adding that it develops its workforce by "strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world."
Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, and Tata did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.
The suspension marks a victory for tech workers who have complained about unfairly losing out on jobs to immigrant workers.
Jobs Now, an advocacy group composed of US citizens working in big tech, celebrated Vance’s announcement on its X account with a video of dancing crabs. The group publicizes otherwise difficult-to-find PERM job postings and says it helped Americans apply to nearly 500,000 jobs across 7,000 employers between last January and this past July.
The organization and its members have also filed complaints against tech companies about alleged abuse of the PERM system, and have called for a number of changes to the employment immigration system. “Every job in America should be offered to an American first, no exceptions,” the group told WIRED in an unsigned statement.
This isn't the first time tech companies have been targeted over PERM. Earlier this year, OpenAI and a company it acquired agreed to settle accusations from the Trump administration about violating rules for the program. Apple reached a similar deal in 2023.
The administration's disparagement of H-1B visas—one of the most common work visas in the US—has sent waves of panic through Silicon Valley since Trump's reelection. Tech companies are some of the H1-B program's biggest users: So far in the fiscal year 2026, the top three employers with the most visas approved are Amazon, Tata, and Infosys.
Microsoft is No. 5, with 3,688 visas approved in 2026; in 2025, 6,258 visas were approved. According to the company, 80 percent of last year's visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees, not to hire new people.
"The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our US workforce," Microsoft’s statement said.
It's unclear if Thursday’s announcement would affect the ability of employees at these companies to apply for H1-B visas themselves. The Office of the Vice President and the Department of Labor did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for clarity on if the suspension would impact those seeking H-1B visas.
"It's one thing if you want to bring in someone like Elon Musk" who aims to "build something great in America," Vance said on Thursday. He equated the current state of the H-1B program to bringing "indentured servants" into the US, taking jobs away from American workers. (Musk, who was born in South Africa, came to the US via Canada to pursue a bachelor's degree at the University of Pennsylvania.)
The announcement came shortly before Trump was set to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. When asked about the upcoming event, Vance said, "We’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.”
Vance also said that the administration is investigating nine universities to see if they might be committing fraud with the J-1 visa program, which allows international candidates to study and conduct research in the US.
“I don’t care how prestigious a university thinks it is, break the law and screw the American people, and I will personally cuff you in the university square," Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said.
Paresh Dave contributed reporting.

Eight technology companies suspended

The suspension affects a process through which US employers must demonstrate that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect wages or job opportunities for American workers.

sources.news_title: Vance Suspends Microsoft Green Card Access Over Visa Abuse
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance suspended Microsoft and other firms from green-card pathways Thursday, accusing tech giants of abusing visas to replace American workers.
Standing with Labor Department leaders, Vance said the Trump administration is cutting Microsoft, Adobe, and a slate of major outsourcing companies off from the Permanent Labor Certification program, known as PERM. That program is the main federal route companies use to sponsor foreign workers for green cards.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the Department will not accept any new PERM applications from the named firms and will not process pending ones. The move hits companies the administration says have flooded the system with foreign-labor requests while American workers lose ground.
Fox Business reported the announcements from the news conference, where officials framed the suspensions as the opening step in a wider crackdown on H-1B and J-1 visa abuse.
Vance zeroed in on Microsoft. He said no company has abused the system more.
Vice President JD Vance put it this way:
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft."
He tied the charge to concrete numbers. Last year, he said, Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
Vance added:
"For every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with 1½ foreign indentured servants."
His message was direct. Microsoft is a great American company, he said, but it has to hire great American workers. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
He returned to the point later, saying Microsoft laid off 6,000 Americans while replacing them with 6,300 H-1B holders. The goal is not to harm the company, Vance said, but to make it thrive by employing fellow Americans.
Microsoft issued a statement soon after the conference. The company said the vast majority of its U.S. employees are Americans and that it looks forward to giving the administration more information.
Of roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year, Microsoft said 80 percent were to extend or change the status of people already on its payroll. Those were not new hires.
The remaining filings for new employees, the company said, covered people already legally in the United States who chose to join Microsoft. Those filings equal only 1 percent of its U.S. workforce and are not new arrivals. Microsoft said it pays H-1B workers the same as others doing comparable work and that its wages rank among the highest in the category.
The company described its model as building the world’s best technology workforce by hiring Americans and attracting top talent from abroad. The administration is not buying the framing.
Sonderling announced the same freeze for Adobe and several large IT outsourcing firms: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini, among others. He linked the step to active federal investigations.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling stated:
"We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies."
The scale he cited is large. Since 2009, he said, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They received more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and more than 100,000 permanent labor certifications.
Sonderling called those hundreds of thousands of jobs taken from American workers. He described the suspensions as the first critical step to stop fraud and abuse and to ensure the programs never come at the expense of the American worker. Under President Trump’s leadership and the task force led with Vance, he said, the administration is ending the fraud that has fueled reliance on foreign labor.
Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito announced a separate track: a historic investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud at nine major universities. The J-1 is an exchange-visitor visa. Officials say some schools have misused the category to dodge normal employment rules.
The schools named are Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, and MIT. D’Esposito said subpoenas have already been served and investigations are underway.
Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said:
"Subpoenas have been served, investigations are underway, and nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building."
He added that improperly using J-1 classifications to avoid employment obligations, exploit taxpayer-funded programs, and undermine American workers will not be tolerated.
Attorney General Todd Blanche warned that companies or individuals found to have broken U.S. law could face criminal cases.
The same effort includes a proposed $100,000 fee on H-1B visa filings. Texas Congresswoman Beth Van Duyne discussed the fee and pointed to systemic abuses, including active fraud investigations in North Texas.
Officials are also weighing an end to H-4 work permits. Those permits let spouses of H-1B holders take jobs in the United States. Former acting ICE Director Jonathan Fahey addressed the economic impact on American workers if that authority is pulled back.
Vance cast the whole system as a broken promise. Visa programs were meant to give American companies access to the best and brightest, he said. Instead they undercut wages and replace U.S. employees.
Vice President JD Vance said:
"This is a fundamental insult to the American worker and to the American way of life."
He called the current setup a terribly pernicious system that has gone on too long and urged Congress to reform it. The administration already has tools to make the programs work better for Americans, he said, and could do far more if Congress is willing to play ball.
Vance extended the invitation to both parties. If lawmakers want the H-1B program to stop defrauding taxpayers and undercutting wages, he said, get to work. In the meantime the administration will use every authority it has to make the program run as designed.
PERM suspensions do not yank existing green cards or instantly deport anyone. They block the named companies from using the federal certification process to lock in more permanent foreign hires through that channel. H-1B remains a temporary specialty-occupation visa; PERM is the bridge many employers use toward lasting status.
By freezing that bridge for Microsoft, Adobe, and the big outsourcing shops, the Labor Department is raising the cost of treating foreign labor as a first resort. The university subpoenas put elite campuses on notice that exchange visas are not a back door around wage and hiring rules.
Sonderling’s multi-year totals, nearly 3 million requests, hundreds of thousands of approvals, show how routine the pipeline became. Vance’s Microsoft numbers put a single-company face on the same pattern: layoffs on one side of the ledger, new foreign visas and green cards on the other.
Microsoft’s reply stresses that most of its recent H-1B paper was for people already inside the company and that new filings are a thin slice of its U.S. headcount. The administration’s reply is that the overall volume still crowds out Americans and that the program’s original purpose has been warped.
No injuries, arrests, or facility closures were announced. The immediate consequences are administrative: closed PERM doors for the listed firms, live investigations, served subpoenas, a proposed six-figure H-1B fee, and a live debate over spouse work permits. Criminal referrals remain possible if evidence supports them.
The open questions are real. The precise legal instrument behind the PERM freeze was not detailed at the podium. Specific evidence against each company and each university was not laid out in public. Adobe’s full response was not yet on the record beyond outreach. The calendar date attached to “Thursday” was not fixed in the initial reports. Those gaps do not erase the action itself.
What landed Thursday is a clear shift in enforcement posture. The White House and Labor Department are treating high-volume visa use by major tech and outsourcing players as a threat to American wages and jobs, not as neutral global talent management. They are daring Congress to revise the statutes while they tighten the screws with the tools already on the books.
American workers should not have to compete with a federal pipeline that makes them optional. When companies and campuses treat visa programs as a discount labor channel, the administration is right to shut the spigot.

sources.news_title: JD Vance suspends Microsoft from H-1B visa usage – The Horn News
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s administration, led by Vice President J.D. Vance’s efforts on immigration, is suspending tech giant Microsoft from a program to apply for green cards for workers who come to the U.S. to live and work using H-1B visas as it accuses the company of fraud.
Supporters of the Republican president have long argued that various programs like the one Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing essentially empower American companies to recruit foreign workers for jobs that end up undercutting Americans. In a wide-ranging announcement Thursday, Vance and other top administration officials also called out universities over their use of J-1 visas for international students and information technology outsourcing firms.
The announcement came hours before Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, part of an event at which he is granting some of the nation’s most prestigious science and technology awards to his tech billionaire allies.
Vance says US workers are replaced with ‘foreign indentured servants’
Vance said the program from which Microsoft is being suspended requires companies to advertise jobs in America before applying to the Department of Labor to show they need to give a foreign worker a green card because of a lack of American workers.
“They’ll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that ‘We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.’ And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft.”
Microsoft is No. 5 among U.S. employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according data from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No. 1.
Microsoft, which is based in Redmond, Washington, near Seattle, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at USCIS during the Biden administration, called Vance’s announcement “incoherent.”
“If the Trump administration were truly concerned that H-1B workers are ‘indentured servants,’ then the last thing they would do is block companies from helping their own H-1B workers get green cards,” he said. “Once you have a green card, you’re no longer dependent on your employer for your immigration status — you’re a permanent resident who can change jobs and negotiate higher wages without fear.”
Vance said Microsoft last year laid off 6,000 American workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said in a White House news conference announcing the decision. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”
Vance said H-1B workers are effectively foreign indentured servants because if they lose their job, they have to leave the country, and they earn less than Americans in the same position.
H-1B program has been scrutinized
The H-1B program has long been a target of Trump supporters who say that the program undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.
H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find American workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
Trump last year attempted to ratchet up the fee for H-1B work visas to $100,000, saying it would protect American workers from losing their jobs to lower-paid foreigners, but a federal judge struck that down in June.
The administration has since tried a different tack, announcing plans in August for a $103,265 fee. The proposed regulation described the new fee as a “dedicated revenue mechanism to help recover a portion of the federal government’s costs of administering the lawful immigration system.” The rule isn’t yet final and is expected to face a legal challenge, like the one before it.
Trump also has targeted foreign students
The Vance announcement came a day after Trump’s administration launched another broadside against international students and their ability to work in the U.S.
The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States. The proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the Optional Practical Training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school.
Vance also called out universities that he suggested were abusing a program to allow international students to come to the U.S. These temporary visas, called J-1 visas, allow international visitors to temporarily come to the U.S. for work and study exchange programs. Vance singled out nine universities that he said merited further investigation for J-1 visa fraud, saying they used the program in greater proportions than their counterparts.
The universities were Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech; Arizona State; and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or MIT.
The Associated Press contributed to this article

sources.news_title: Trump Admin Blocks Microsoft, Adobe and Six Other Tech Companies From Green Card Program › American Greatness
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance announced Thursday that the Trump administration has blocked Microsoft, Adobe, and six other IT outsourcing firms from using the U.S. Department of Labor’s green card program, citing alleged fraud, misuse of H-1B and J-1 visas, and the displacement of American workers.
The suspension bars these companies from submitting new applications to the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM), or having pending applications processed. The ban will remain in place “as long as it needs to be,” Vance said.
The vice president also announced federal investigations into nine universities—Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, and MIT—for visa fraud and undercutting American citizens.
“These universities are employing J-1 visas for federally funded grants at a rate of about 61 percent,” said Vance. “The national average is 38 percent. So something weird is going on at these universities!”
Vance, flanked by Department of Labor (DOL) Secretary Keith Sonderling, DOL Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito, Attorney General Todd Blanche, senior Trump advisor Stephen Miller, and Anti-Fraud Task Force Vice Chair Andrew Ferguson, made the announcements during a press conference at the White House, Thursday.
PERM is a mandatory first step for most employers seeking to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards.
In addition to Microsoft and Adobe, the administration ha suspended Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini from using the program.
“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers,” said Sonderling. “They’ve received over 230,000 H1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications—”That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers!”
The vice president specifically called out Microsoft for laying off 6,000 US workers, while hiring 6,300 foreign workers with H1-B visas.
“This is a fundamental insult to the American worker and to the American way of life,” said Vance. We cannot allow visa programs that were designed to ensure that American corporations had access to the best and the brightest, to use them to undercut the wages of American workers!”
The VP clarified that the policy is not meant to bar people like Elon Musk from coming into the country, “but if you’re bringing in an accountant who’s making $40,000 a year and you use that foreign indentured servant making to replace an American worker who was making $70,000 a year, you’re not bringing in a genius to build a great American corporation. You’re committing fraud!”
He added that “no company has abused this more than Microsoft.”
H-1B visas allow U.S. employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations, generally requiring at least a bachelor’s degree or its equivalent. J-1 visas are issued to exchange visitors approved for work- and study-based programs in the United States.
Vance said he would support eliminating the H-1B program entirely, calling it “completely broken,” while acknowledging that the government must protect American workers as long as the program remains in place.
Miller told reporters that companies been abusing the visa programs to exploit low skill foreign workers.
“In case after case after case, we see individuals that are being brought into the country for skills that are not specialized, that are not unique, and that are not skilled, and that are doing work that is currently being done by American workers, but a vastly lower pay,” he explained. “Historic volumes of food stamp fraud, daycare fraud, Medicaid fraud, health care fraud, Social Security fraud. Every kind of fraud you can imagine that steals from and betrays American families!”
Miller stated the abuse amounts to “systemic immigration fraud that violates the laws and statutes of the United States to undercut American workers and labor.”
Vance said the nine universities under investigation have been using the J-1 visas “way too much.”
“They’re using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers. And it simply has to stop,” he said.
DOL Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito emphasized the extent of the J-1 visa abuse among the targeted universities and made clear he intended to put a stop to it.
“Approximately 61 percent postdoctoral researchers and federally funded workers at these institutions are foreign nationals,” he explained, adding that “subpoenas have been served” to the nine universities.
“Any university that commits this BS needs to not only be targeted but cut off from the program and defunded,” D’Esposito stated. “These schools sit on billions in endowments and still take our tax dollars, then hand those research jobs to cheaper foreign labor,” he continued. “American students are getting squeezed out of their own country’s labs!”
D’Esposito stressed that the Ivory Tower is no longer immune to public scrutiny.
“I will personally handcuff you in the university square!” he declared. “I spent a career as a NYPD detective—I did not back down then, and I sure as hell will not back down now. I don’t care how prestigious a university thinks it is! I don’t care how large your endowment is, how powerful your alumni are, or how many politicians you have on speed dial.”
Andrew Ferguson, the anti-fraud task force chair, emphasized the Trump administration’s “America First” philosophy.
“America is not a jobs program for the rest of the world,” said Ferguson. “We didn’t build our institutions for the rest of the world. We built them for Americans.”
He praised Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) Chair Andrea Lucas for addressing issues previous EEOCs “refused to touch,” including protecting white American men from discrimination, and protecting American citizens from national origin discrimination.
“She has led the EEOC headlong to defend Americans from these abusive practices,” Ferguson said, calling her the greatest EEOC chairman since Clarence Thomas in the 1980s.
The vice president discouraged foreigners from coming to the United States to take advantage of “our very generous welfare system.”
“If your purpose in coming to the United States of America is to cash a check from our generous welfare program, then you’re not going to enrich the United States of America and we would prefer that you do not come here,” he said.
When asked to comment on Socialism is, Vance noted that it is a hard term to define because it keeps mutating.
“Classically, you would think socialism is about prioritizing workers, and yet in reality, I guarantee that most of the self-described socialists running across the United States of America are going to howl about this announcement today, which is prioritizing American workers over foreign workers,” he said. “I think in reality what it actually means in the American context is that you want to replace American workers with foreign workers, and you want boys to play in girls sports,” Vance added.
The VP went on to slam socialist Senator Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) for opposing open borders ten years ago because it provided cheap labor, but attacking President Trump now for closing the border to protect American workers.
“It is ironic that so many of the self-described socialists running across this country, they love the idea of replacing American workers with foreign workers,” Vance said. “[For them], it’s not about the working class. It’s about their hatred of native-born citizens!”

sources.news_title: US freezes green-card processing for Microsoft, Adobe workers
sources.text:
The United States government has suspended the processing of employment-based green-card applications involving major technology companies, including Microsoft and Adobe, over alleged abuse of the country’s skilled-worker immigration system, Reuters reports on Thursday.
The move, which also affects major information technology companies such as Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant and Capgemini, is part of the Trump administration’s wider crackdown on employment-based immigration.
According to Reuters, the US Labour Department will stop accepting new applications and processing pending applications for permanent labour certification involving the named companies.
The certification, known as PERM, is required for many employers seeking to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residence in the US.
Employers must generally demonstrate that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of American workers.
US Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the system more than any other US company, pointing to layoffs at the technology giant while it continued to use the H-1B visa programme and seek green cards for foreign workers.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” Vance said at a press conference on Thursday.
He stated, “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.
“You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
Reuters reports that Microsoft disputed the suggestion that it was using the programme to replace American workers, saying about 80 per cent of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were for existing employees seeking extensions or changes of status rather than new hires.
The company also said H-1B workers were paid the same as comparable employees.
The Labour Secretary, Keith Sonderling, said the suspension covered the eight named companies and would remain in place as the administration investigated their use of the permanent labour certification system.
“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.
The companies have collectively sought nearly three million foreign workers since 2009, with more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications, according to Labour Department data cited by Reuters.
The action comes weeks after the Trump administration introduced a $100,000 fee for new H-1B petitions involving workers hired from abroad.
The administration’s Project Firewall has also opened about 200 cases and imposed millions of dollars in penalties as it investigates alleged violations involving the hiring of foreign workers.
The administration has accused some employers of posting ineffective job advertisements and then claiming that qualified American workers could not be found, allowing them to hire foreign workers at lower wages.
The companies affected by the latest action have not been found guilty of those allegations.
The freeze is therefore focused on employment-based immigration and does not mean that existing green-card holders or all immigrants in the US have lost their status.
The administration has also opened investigations into nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, over alleged misuse of exchange-visitor visas.
Vance said the university investigations were aimed at examining whether foreign workers and students were being used to undercut American wages, while the administration is also investigating alleged foreign influence and visa abuses.
The latest actions are part of President Donald Trump’s broader immigration policy, which has placed greater pressure on US employers to hire American workers rather than rely on foreign labour.

sources.news_title: Vance says H-1B program ‘rife with fraud’ as Labor suspends Microsoft, major IT firms
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — Vice President JD Vance said Thursday the H-1B visa program has become “rife with fraud,” as the Labor Department suspended Microsoft, Adobe and several of the world’s largest information-technology outsourcing firms from the permanent labor certification process.
Speaking at a White House press conference on visa fraud, Vance said the program was created for a narrow purpose and has used to displace American workers.
“The H-1B visa program is meant to allow companies to bring in really the best of the best from outside the United States of America for positions that are completely impossible to fill with American workers,” Vance said. “Unfortunately, the program has become rife with fraud.”
Vance, who leads President Donald Trump’s White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, singled out Microsoft.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” he said.
The White House said Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025 after certifying that it could not find qualified American employees, while the company was approved for more than 6,000 H-1B visas and filed 3,682 applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, known as PERM. Nearly 1,000 of those applications were for the same positions the administration said were held by the laid-off American workers, officials said.
PERM is the Labor Department process employers use to seek permanent residency for foreign workers. The approval process generally requires employers to test the U.S. labor market and certify that there are no qualified U.S. workers available for the position.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department is cutting off that path for firms the administration says are connected to the alleged abuse.
“I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini, and also, due to multiple active federal investigations, the Department of Labor is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the program,” Sonderling said.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said the action is meant as a warning to other companies beyond those named Thursday.
“This announcement today should send and does send a strong signal to every single employer in the United States that the Trump administration will not tolerate discrimination against American workers,” Blanche said.
White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller tied the visa actions to the broader fraud task force Trump put under Vance.
“Since President Trump launched the Fraud Task Force and put the Vice President in charge, our worst nightmares about the fraud that had been taking place in this country were exceeded, fraud that has been going on for years, decades and, in some cases, generations,” Miller said.
The Labor Department’s inspector general separately announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud at nine universities: the University of Pittsburgh, Yale, Harvard, Stanford, Brown, the University of California, Davis, the California Institute of Technology, Arizona State University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
“I am announcing a historic investigation into the J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities,” the inspector general said. “Subpoenas have been served; investigations are underway.”
The J-1 program covers exchange visitors, including researchers and students. Officials did not detail the allegations against the schools.
Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson framed the crackdown as a question of whom the programs are supposed to serve.
“America is not a jobs program for the rest of the world. We didn’t build our institutions for the rest of the world, we built them for Americans,” Ferguson said.
The H-1B program lets U.S. employers hire foreign workers in specialty occupations, generally jobs that require at least a bachelor’s degree. Congress caps most new visas at 85,000 a year, though universities and some research employers are exempt from the cap, and existing visa holders can extend their status. Employers seeking green cards for those workers typically must first obtain a PERM certification from the Labor Department.
Thursday’s suspensions bar the named companies from obtaining new permanent-labor certifications while investigations continue. Officials did not say how long the suspensions will last or whether criminal charges will follow.

sources.text:
The U.S. Department of Labor is barring Microsoft $MSFT and Adobe $ADBE from the Permanent Labor Certification program — a pathway to permanent residency for skilled foreign workers — because of ongoing federal investigations into the companies. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspensions on Thursday, according to CNBC.
Sonderling said the Labor Department is closing the door on new permanent labor certification filings for Microsoft, Adobe, and a set of large IT outsourcing companies — Cognizant, Infosys, Capgemini, Tata, Wipro, and HCL.
"Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers," Sonderling said, according to CNBC.
Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft at the news conference, pointing to the company's 6,000 layoffs in 2025. Vance claimed Microsoft had "replaced" those workers with H-1B visa holders. "So we're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we're also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first," Vance said, according to CNBC.
Microsoft pushed back on that characterization. In a statement, the company said that of the roughly 6,000 H-1B visa applications it submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% were to extend or change the status of existing employees — not to hire new workers. The remaining filings covered individuals already in the United States and represent only 1% of Microsoft's U.S. workforce, the company said. Microsoft also noted that compensation for its H-1B workers is on par with what it pays other staff in equivalent roles, and that its H-1B wage levels rank among the highest recorded across all such petitions.
Adobe did not respond to requests for comment, according to CNBC and TechCrunch.
The announcement came at the same event where President Donald Trump had been slated to present the National Medal of Science to Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and other tech leaders, according to CNBC.
H-1B visas exist to give employers access to foreign talent for specialized roles where the domestic labor pool is deemed insufficient. Nearly three-quarters of approved H-1B visas go to workers from India, according to TechCrunch. According to 2026 data from Levels.fyi cited by CNBC, Microsoft ranked fourth among H-1B sponsors this year with 21,706 petitions and a median base salary of $180,710.
