sources.news_title: Vance: Microsoft suspended from PERM green card sponsorship program
Trump Administration Blocks Microsoft, Adobe and Six Tech Giants From Green Card Program Over Alleged Hiring Abuses
sources.text:
The Labor Department has suspended eight major technology and outsourcing companies from sponsoring foreign employees for permanent residency, citing alleged misuse of immigration programs and concerns that American workers are being displaced.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration announced Thursday, Oct. 8, that eight major technology and information technology outsourcing companies will be barred from submitting new permanent labor certification applications or advancing pending cases, escalating federal efforts to prioritize American workers in the technology industry.
Vice President JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the restrictions during a White House news conference, identifying Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini as companies suspended from the Permanent Labor Certification Program, commonly known as PERM.
The decision immediately affects a major pathway through which employers sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards. Federal officials accused the companies of taking advantage of immigration programs while American technology professionals face layoffs and competition for available positions.
The administration’s action does not constitute a blanket prohibition on hiring foreign nationals or automatically revoke existing H-1B visas. Instead, it prevents the affected employers from obtaining the labor certifications generally required to sponsor foreign employees for permanent residency through certain employment-based immigration categories.
As reported by The Hill following the White House announcement, Vance singled out Microsoft, accusing the company of making extensive use of foreign labor programs while eliminating American jobs.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said.
The vice president said the administration supports continued investment and expansion in the American technology industry but expects corporations benefiting from the U.S. economy to provide more employment opportunities to domestic workers.
“We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector. We are the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers,” Vance said.
The announcement represents one of the administration’s most significant actions against corporate participation in employment-based immigration programs, targeting both American technology companies and multinational outsourcing firms that employ substantial numbers of foreign professionals.
Sonderling said the Labor Department would stop accepting new PERM applications from the designated employers and suspend processing of applications already submitted.
“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” the labor secretary said.
The suspension applies to six major outsourcing companies — Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini — as well as Microsoft and Adobe.
Sonderling said Microsoft and Adobe were being suspended amid multiple active federal investigations, while the administration’s broader enforcement effort also targets outsourcing companies whose recruitment and employment practices have drawn scrutiny.
The government has not publicly established that every company named committed fraud, and the announcement itself does not constitute a final judicial finding of wrongdoing.
However, federal officials maintain that employment and immigration records demonstrate patterns warranting immediate restrictions.
Sonderling cited figures covering the period since 2009, saying the eight companies collectively sought authorization to employ millions of foreign workers.
“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They’ve received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications,” Sonderling said.
“That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” he added.
The figures were presented by the administration as evidence of the companies’ extensive participation in foreign labor programs.
However, the number of visa petitions or labor certifications does not independently establish that an equivalent number of American workers lost employment. Determining displacement would require evidence concerning particular job openings, qualified domestic applicants, hiring decisions and whether positions would otherwise have been filled by U.S. workers.
Some applications may also involve extensions, changes in employment circumstances or different stages of a foreign worker’s immigration process.
Nevertheless, the scale of the filings has become central to the administration’s argument that existing immigration rules have been used to the disadvantage of American technology professionals.
The PERM process is administered by the Department of Labor and serves as an initial step for many employment-based green card applications.
Before sponsoring a foreign worker for certain permanent positions, employers generally must demonstrate that they have conducted required recruitment efforts and that there are no qualified, willing, available and able U.S. workers for the position at the prevailing wage.
The process also requires employers to establish that hiring the foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers.
Once certification is approved, the employer may proceed with an immigrant petition through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Additional requirements, including visa availability and eligibility for adjustment of status or consular processing, must be satisfied before a worker can obtain permanent residency.
Because labor certification is required for many employment-based green card categories, suspending access to PERM can substantially disrupt companies’ ability to sponsor foreign employees for permanent residence.
The consequences may be particularly significant for workers who are already employed in the United States under temporary visas and are relying on their employers to sponsor them for green cards.
For many technology professionals, the H-1B visa is the initial employment authorization used before pursuing permanent residency.
The H-1B program permits eligible U.S. employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations that generally require specialized knowledge and a qualifying educational background.
Technology companies and information technology consulting firms have historically been among the program’s largest users.
The administration’s new PERM restrictions are distinct from the H-1B program itself, although the two systems frequently intersect when an employer sponsors an existing H-1B employee for permanent residence.
Without access to PERM, affected companies could face obstacles advancing certain employees toward green cards, even if those workers retain valid temporary employment authorization.
The precise implications will depend on individual immigration circumstances, including visa validity, previously approved petitions and whether another employment-based pathway is available.
Federal officials have not announced when the suspensions might be lifted or what requirements the companies would need to satisfy to regain access.
The policy could affect thousands of foreign technology workers, particularly those from India who face lengthy employment-based green card backlogs because of annual numerical limits and country-specific allocation rules.
Large outsourcing companies, including Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro, have built extensive operations serving American businesses through software development, technical support, consulting and other information technology services.
Their participation in temporary and permanent employment immigration programs has generated repeated disagreements over whether foreign labor supplements the domestic workforce or allows employers to reduce labor costs.
Critics of the programs argue that some companies use foreign workers to fill positions that qualified Americans could perform, potentially weakening bargaining power and suppressing wages.
Employers and supporters of skilled immigration maintain that access to international talent helps address shortages in specialized occupations, supports innovation and enables companies to expand U.S. operations.
Both arguments depend on labor market conditions, the occupations involved and the employment practices of individual companies.
The latest restrictions are being introduced against a backdrop of layoffs and restructuring throughout the American technology sector.
Major companies have reduced staffing in certain divisions while increasing spending on artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure and other emerging technologies.
Those simultaneous trends have created disagreements over whether employers should receive permission to sponsor additional foreign workers while some experienced American professionals struggle to find new positions.
Vance directly addressed those concerns, arguing that technology companies should not replace dismissed U.S. employees with foreign workers.
“Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” he said, according to Reuters’ reporting on the announcement.
“You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants,” Vance added.
The vice president’s remarks reflect the administration’s position that foreign labor programs require stronger enforcement to prevent employers from using immigration status as a means of obtaining less expensive or more dependent workers.
The White House announcement also included additional investigations involving American universities accused of potentially misusing exchange visitor programs.
Sonderling said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would face investigations concerning their use of J-1 visas.
Other institutions identified in reporting about the initiative include the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Brown University.
The J-1 exchange visitor program permits eligible foreign nationals to participate in approved educational, research, training and cultural exchange activities.
Federal officials are examining whether participating universities have used the program in ways that could undermine wages or displace American workers.
Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas had already been served as part of the investigations.
“We will investigate whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research,” D’Esposito said.
“If an American university is breaking the law to save $1 while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It’s institutional betrayal.”
The allegations concerning the universities remain under investigation, and the announcement did not establish that the institutions had been found guilty of violating federal law.
The action against technology companies follows several other initiatives undertaken by the Trump administration to increase oversight of employment-based immigration.
Federal officials have sought to tighten requirements involving H-1B visas, revise immigration fee structures and increase scrutiny of programs allowing international students and other foreign nationals to work in the United States.
The administration has also announced enforcement efforts aimed at identifying fraudulent labor certifications and ensuring that employers comply with required recruitment procedures.
One such initiative, known as Project Firewall, was established to strengthen investigations into potential H-1B program abuses and expand the Labor Department’s role in identifying employers suspected of violating wage and labor requirements.
The administration has additionally imposed a $100,000 payment requirement on certain new H-1B petitions, a measure intended to discourage employers from relying on foreign workers when American candidates are available.
Those changes have drawn criticism from business organizations and immigration advocates who argue that additional restrictions could increase costs and interfere with companies’ ability to recruit workers with specialized technical expertise.
Supporters of the administration’s policies counter that existing immigration pathways must be enforced in a manner that prevents wage suppression and protects American applicants.
The decision to suspend major companies from PERM marks a further escalation because it directly restricts access to a critical stage of employment-based permanent immigration.
The announcement also attracted substantial attention from conservative commentators who described the restrictions as a fulfillment of Trump’s campaign promises to prioritize domestic employment.
Eric Daugherty, chief content officer at Right Line News and Florida’s Voice, highlighted the administration’s announcement in an Oct. 8 statement, identifying the eight affected companies and emphasizing the government’s figures on foreign labor applications.
“JUST IN: Effective immediately the Trump administration has hereby SUSPENDED ADOBE, MICROSOFT, Cognizant, Tata, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini from the Permanent Labor Certification Program,” Daugherty wrote.
“They undercut American workers. THEY FAFO’D,” he added.
Daugherty described the action as “MASSIVE” and argued that the affected companies had relied on foreign labor programs for years.
“A flurry of companies, including some of the biggest outsourcing giants on the planet. Tata, Infosys, Wipro, and HCL have been H1B pipelines for YEARS,” he wrote.
“Without PERM, they can’t sponsor foreign workers for green cards. The path to keep them here for good is SHUT!”
He credited Vance, White House adviser Stephen Miller and D’Esposito with implementing the administration’s labor priorities.
“Vance, Stephen Miller, and IG D’Esposito are delivering exactly what Trump promised in 2024!” Daugherty wrote. “HIRE AMERICAN, IT IS THAT SIMPLE.”
While the suspension prevents the companies from advancing PERM labor certifications during the restriction, it does not necessarily eliminate every possible legal pathway to permanent residency for their foreign employees.
Some workers may qualify for immigration categories that do not require PERM certification, while others could potentially seek sponsorship through different employers.
Those distinctions will become important as affected employees and companies assess the practical implications of the Labor Department’s decision.
Microsoft and Adobe did not immediately provide substantive public responses to the allegations when contacted by news organizations following the announcement.
Other affected companies also had not publicly detailed how they intended to respond to the restrictions or whether they would pursue administrative or judicial remedies.
The Labor Department has not published a comprehensive breakdown of alleged violations associated with each company, nor has it established a public timetable for completing the investigations.
Those details could influence whether the suspensions remain in effect for an extended period or are modified following additional reviews.
For American technology professionals, the administration is presenting the decision as an effort to increase access to positions that might otherwise be filled through employment-based immigration programs.
Whether the restrictions result in additional domestic hiring will depend on how the affected companies respond, whether they expand recruitment of U.S. workers and how changes to permanent labor certification influence broader staffing decisions.
The suspension could also lead employers to restructure hiring arrangements, relocate certain operations or seek different immigration pathways, outcomes that remain uncertain.
The immediate change is that eight major technology and outsourcing companies can no longer use the Labor Department’s PERM process to advance new or pending labor certifications under the announced restrictions.
The decision gives the administration additional leverage over corporate immigration practices while increasing scrutiny of employment arrangements involving foreign technology workers.
As federal investigators examine the companies’ recruitment histories and immigration filings, the Labor Department’s next steps will determine whether the restrictions lead to further enforcement actions, negotiated compliance measures or legal challenges.
For now, the Trump administration has made one of its strongest interventions yet in the employment-based immigration system, placing major technology employers on notice that continued access to foreign labor programs will face heightened scrutiny over their treatment of American workers.

sources.news_title: Trump honors Microsoft’s CEO after Vance drops an H-1B visa hammer on the company
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump celebrated tech billionaires for their contributions to America on Thursday only hours after a company run by one of them, Microsoft, was accused by his vice president of abusing the visa system to bring in more foreign workers.
It so happens five of the six leaders he honored are immigrants.
Before the ceremony that recognized Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Vice President JD Vance announced at a news conference that the tech company was being suspended from a program that allows companies to apply for green cards for skilled foreign workers with H-1B visas.
The crackdown on Microsoft revealed the tension between the companies that power U.S. economic growth and the administration’s efforts to reduce immigration. Trump’s team insists it’s possible to spot the superstar immigrants who could lead groundbreaking companies and says hiring unexceptional foreigners has hurt U.S. workers.
“Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance told a news conference. He said the company had abused the visa system. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
Vance said Microsoft last year fired 6,000 U.S. workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
The tech company, based in Redmond, Washington, has 223,000 employees worldwide. It said in a statement that the majority of its H-1B visa applications last fiscal year were “to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
In presenting the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft’s CEO, Trump took a more flattering approach and made no statements about the company’s hiring of foreign workers.
“For more than three decades, Satya Nadella has been a key figure in the transformation of Microsoft, revolutionizing the company and empowering businesses, students and consumers from all over the world with some of the most capable software ever built,” Trump said.
When Vance was asked about the seeming contradiction, he said, “We’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft.”
Of the six tech leaders who received an award for scientific and technological achievement from the president, five came from abroad.
The president gave the National Medal of Science to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Lisa Su, CEO of the semiconductor company Advanced Micro Devices. Each of them was born overseas — South Africa for Musk, Russia for Brin and Taiwan for Huang and Su.
In addition to Nadella, Trump also gave the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, who has sponsored the government’s special investment accounts for children known as Trump Accounts. Dell was born in Texas, while Nadella immigrated from India.
On social media, Nadella thanked Trump.
“I’m humbled to stand alongside so many giants of American innovation and looking forward for what we can continue to do together to advance technology and drive American prosperity,” he posted.
They’re praised as ‘national treasures’
Trump called the group of billionaires “national treasures,” comparing them to his uncle, John Trump, an electrical engineer and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who received the National Medal of Science in 1983.
“Such a big day in the world of science and the world of technology — this is the biggest day there is,” Trump said. “You’re going to go down in the annals of history as being great.”
The honors — part of a summit celebrating a new “golden age” of science — build on Trump’s already lavish praise toward the entrepreneurs for their work accelerating the development of artificial intelligence technology, which he refers to as super intelligence. He has increasingly counted on the technology to deliver on his economic agenda and pushed for the U.S. to lead its development while resisting calls for guardrails that he worries will stifle growth.
“We have an extremely high IQ audience, for a change,” Trump joked to the event’s attendees.
Past winners of the National Medal of Science, which was established in 1959, have mainly been academics and research scientists rather than business leaders. The ceremony honoring the business leaders overlaps with the awarding this week, separately, of Nobel Prizes.
The tech leaders have been frequent visitors to the White House in recent weeks. Musk, Huang and Su sat at the head table with Trump at the lavish state dinner for China’s leader, Xi Jinping. Also attending were Brin, Nadella and Dell, who on Wednesday was in the Oval Office to talk about Trump Accounts.
Last week, Huang and Musk were among the tech leaders at the White House to sign a voluntary agreement on developing AI after recent models raised national security and safety concerns.
With November’s midterm elections less than a month away, Trump has also sought to drive home to voters how investment in AI data centers and related computer equipment has helped to boost a record-high stock market, swelling the net worth of wealthier Americans. But the message hasn’t always landed. Polls show bipartisan concerns about AI developing too quickly, and high costs for everyday items like gas and groceries are dampening the economic outlook for many Americans.
Vance also said that several universities including Stanford and MIT should be investigated for visa fraud. Huang and Brin have degrees from Stanford and Su has multiple degrees from MIT.
The White House praised the contributions of Thursday’s honorees.
“These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation,” said Liz Huston, a White House spokesperson.

sources.text:

Visa probe also targets universities for allegedly exploiting international students to reduce US wage costs.
The United States government is suspending several major tech companies, including Adobe and Microsoft, from a programme that gives skilled foreign workers a path to permanent residency amid allegations of fraud.
The move comes as the White House ramps up pressure on companies to hire more Americans. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” US Vice President JD Vance said at a news conference on Thursday.
Vance claimed that the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant laid off 6,000 American workers while obtaining 6,300 H-1B foreign work visas and almost 3,000 permanent residencies known as green cards.
“You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.
Across the technology sector, there have been more than 131,000 layoffs in 2026 alone, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job cuts across the tech and startup industries.
“When someone comes in, they are completely subordinate to that company. If they lose that job, they have to leave the country.”
Microsoft pushed back on Vance’s claims in a blog post, saying that “80 percent of the visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
“The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said in the post.
Microsoft is No 5 among US employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No 1.
Adobe did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling also said that several major information technology firms will be suspended from the programme as well. Among them are Indian tech giants Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services.
The H-1B programme has long been a target of supporters of US President Donald Trump who say that the programme undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.
H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find US workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
The Department of Labor also said it had uncovered $22bn worth of visa fraud.
“Today we are protecting something far more valuable than any dollar amount. We are protecting the American worker,” Sonderling said.
The news came hours before Trump was to honour Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. India-born Nadella was one of six business leaders to be awarded on Thursday. Five of the leaders were foreign-born, including Tesla boss Elon Musk and Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Crackdown on universities
During the news conference, officials also announced a crackdown on alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine universities, including MIT, Harvard, Yale, Stanford and Cal State, amid allegations that they brought in international students to undercut US wages. A J-1 visa allows foreign nationals to enter the US temporarily for education or cultural programmes. Universities use these visas to bring in international PhD candidates or scholars.
Vance claimed that when schools employ an American as a researcher, that person earns $20,000 more than someone brought in under a J-1 visa.
Al Jazeera asked for data supporting this claim, but the White House did not respond.
Microsoft’s stock slumped 1.5 percent on the heels of the news, while Adobe was up 2.1 percent in late day trading on Thursday.

sources.text:
White House targets tech giants with H-1B visa suspension
Vice President J.D. Vance calls Microsoft the "biggest abuser" as the administration freezes new and pending H-1B and PERM applications for eight companies.
EDITOR'S NOTE: This story has been updated with comments from Microsoft.
The Trump administration has barred multiple technology companies from hiring workers from outside the U.S. under the H-1B visa program.
At the top of the administration's list is Microsoft, which Vice President J.D. Vance called the "biggest abuser" of the program. Microsoft laid off 6,000 workers in 2015 while adding 6,300 people via the H-1B visa program and another 3,000 workers with Green Cards, Vance said at a White House briefing Thursday.
Microsoft pushed back in a statement Thursday afternoon, saying about 80% of its roughly 6,000 H-1B applications in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers.
Other companies under suspension include Adobe, Cognizant, Tata, Wipro, Infosys, HCL and Capgemini.
“We are cutting off the head of the snake,” Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said in the briefing.
Vance said the administration’s fraud task force has launched multiple criminal investigations, but the abuse of the foreign worker programs is so severe that action could not wait.
The government will not process new or pending applications for H-1B visas and Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, the Labor Department process that is typically the first step for an employer sponsoring a worker for a green card.
“H-1B is how they get in, and PERM program is how they stay,” Vance said.
The White House is claiming rampant fraud in the program that goes back decades.
“H-1B was meant to bring in the best of the best of foreign workers for positions that are impossible to fill with American workers,” Vance said.
Vance said companies will advertise for open positions and then claim no American workers applied, then "go and replace them with indentured servants."
Worker abuse has long been a complaint aimed at the H-1B program because the company, not the individual, holds the visa. That can make it difficult for someone to switch jobs or file complaints.
“They don’t come in with the same rights as an American citizen or American employee. They are being mistreated by their employers and are used to undercut the wages of American workers,” Vance said.
Many of the targeted companies are also federal contractors.
Microsoft is one of the government's largest software suppliers. Cognizant, Capgemini, Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL all perform federal IT services work directly or through U.S. subsidiaries.
It is not clear yet whether the suspension affects workers assigned to government contracts.
We have reached out to Microsoft and will update this story when they respond.
In its statement, Microsoft said its remaining H-1B filings for new hires were for people already legally in the United States, and that those hires equal about 1% of its U.S. workforce.
“They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said.
Microsoft also said it pays H-1B employees the same as other employees doing comparable work, and that its H-1B wages are among the highest of any filer.
The company said the vast majority of its U.S. employees are Americans and that it looks forward to giving the administration more information.

sources.news_title: US suspends IT giants from green card programme
sources.text:
The US government has taken decisive action by suspending major IT firms like Microsoft, Tata, Infosys, and Wipro from the green card application programme, citing concerns over American job displacement and systemic abuse of visa processes.
Key Points
- The US on Thursday suspended eight IT firms, including Microsoft, Tata, Infosys, and Wipro, from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme for green cards.
- The suspension aims to address concerns that these firms have shut out American workers from the job market.
- Microsoft and Adobe were suspended due to multiple active federal investigations, with Vice President Vance accusing Microsoft of significant abuse of the system, including laying off 6,000 American workers in 2025 while seeking foreign workers for similar roles.
- The Department of Labour will not accept or process new or pending permanent labour certification applications for the suspended companies.
- An investigation has also been launched into the J-1 visa programme used by nine major universities, including Yale and Harvard, for potentially undercutting American researchers' wages.
The United States on Thursday suspended eight IT firms, including Microsoft, Tata, Infosys and Wipro, from a programme to apply for green cards for foreign workers, contending that the practice has shut out Americans from the job market.
The announcement was made by Vice President J D Vance, Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling, and Attorney General Todd Blanche as part of the action under the aegis of the US Anti-Fraud Task Force.
Major IT Firms Suspended From Green Card Programme
"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," Sonderling said.
He said the Department of Labour is also suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the programme due to multiple active federal investigations.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
"Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025 after certifying that it could not find qualified American employees -- yet the company was approved for more than 6,000 H-1Bs and filed 3,682 PERM applications, including nearly 1,000 applications for the same positions as the laid off American workers," the vice president said.
Impact On Labour Certification Applications
Sonderling said the Department of Labour will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies.
"Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications," Sonderling said.
That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers, Sonderling said.
Indian professionals account for over 70 per cent of all approved H-1B petitions annually.
The Vice President referred to foreign workers hired on H1-B visas as 'foreign indentured servants' and the companies using the programme as 'visa mills'.
Investigation Into University Visa Programmes
Vance also announced an investigation into the J-1 visa programme for research scholars utilised by nine major universities, including Yale, Harvard, Stanford and Caltech.
"Something weird is going on at these universities. They're using these visas way too much. They're using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers," Vance said.
The J-1 programme allows foreign nationals to enter the US as exchange visitors for activities, including research, teaching, study and specialised professional work.
"This is a fundamental insult to the American worker and to the American way of life. We cannot allow visa programs that were designed to ensure that American corporations had access to the best and the brightest, to use them to undercut the wages of American workers," Vance said.
"I don't care how prestigious the university thinks it is. Break the law and screw the American people, and I will personally cuff you in the university square," Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito, Department of Labour, said.
"I don't care how large your endowment is, how powerful your alumni are, or how many politicians you have on speed dial. As Vice President Vance said, nobody is above the law. That's why we're establishing a visa fraud strike team, bringing together investigative expertise from across government," D'Esposito said.

The PERM programme allows employers to demonstrate that no qualified and available American workers can fill certain positions before sponsoring foreign employees for permanent residency.
The suspension is the latest move by President Donald Trump’s administration to tighten employment-based immigration rules and encourage companies to recruit more American workers.
The decision could have significant implications for Indian technology professionals, many of whom work in the United States on H-1B visas and rely on employer sponsorship to obtain green cards.
Indian IT companies have long been major participants in the US technology services market, employing thousands of professionals in software development, consulting and other specialised roles.
The companies named in Thursday’s announcement include Tata, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, Cognizant and Capgemini, alongside Microsoft and Adobe.
While the suspension affects a critical stage of the employment-based green card process, it does not automatically cancel existing H-1B visas or green cards already issued to employees.
The government has not specified how many workers could be affected or how long the restrictions will remain in place.
PERM stands for Permanent Labour Certification. It is a US Department of Labour process that employers generally must complete before sponsoring foreign workers for certain employment-based green cards.

The Labour Department says it will stop processing pending PERM applications involving these companies and will not accept new ones during the suspension.
Will existing H-1B visas be cancelled?

What about workers who already have green cards?
The announcement does not revoke green cards already granted.
How long will the suspension last?

Why does this matter for Indians?

Vice-President JD Vance singled out Microsoft, accusing the technology giant of exploiting immigration rules to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign employees.
Speaking at a White House news conference, Vance alleged that Microsoft had laid off 6,000 American workers last year while obtaining 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.

Under the PERM system, employers seeking permanent residency for foreign workers must first obtain certification from the US Department of Labor.

The suspension means the named companies cannot currently move forward with new or pending PERM applications, potentially delaying permanent residency plans for employees who depend on employer sponsorship.
However, PERM is distinct from the H-1B programme, which allows employers to hire foreign professionals temporarily in specialised occupations.
The announcement was part of a wider immigration crackdown that also targeted leading American universities.

- US officials cited alleged fraud and said the move is aimed at ensuring companies prioritise American workers
- The suspensions come as federal investigators pursue broader allegations of foreign-labour fraud, exploitation and abuse of immigration programmes
The US government has suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six major IT outsourcing companies from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, accusing the firms of alleged fraud and seeking to push companies to hire more American workers.
US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the action on Thursday, naming Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini alongside Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said, according to Reuters.
The PERM process requires an employer to obtain certification from the Department of Labour that no qualified, willing and available US worker can fill a particular position. It is required for most employment-based green card applications.
Firms Suspended
Vice President JD Vance said Microsoft was among the companies being targeted as part of the administration’s effort to address what it described as abuse of the foreign-worker system.
“Our message to Microsoft is: You're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a White House event, according to Reuters.
The White House’s Rapid Response account said the administration was suspending Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, while Microsoft and Adobe were being suspended because of “multiple active federal investigations”.
The move does not amount to a finding of wrongdoing against the companies.
Vance's Wage Claim
Vance also sought to make the case for tighter scrutiny of foreign-worker programmes, arguing that they can allow companies to reduce labour costs.
In remarks posted by the White House vice president’s account, Vance said H-1B workers in the US earn about $20,000 less than American citizens in comparable positions, while workers brought in by foreign outsourcing companies earn $48,000 less.
Vance described the practice as companies bringing in foreign workers, laying off American employees and undercutting US wages. Those figures and characterisations were presented by Vance and were not independently established in the supplied sources.
Fraud Investigations
The latest suspensions come as the Labour Department’s inspector general expands investigations into alleged foreign labour fraud, worker exploitation and potential human trafficking.
In a September 18 statement, Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said investigators had already issued dozens of subpoenas and executed search warrants. The department had also suspended visa applications from Cognizant and Cloudera pending a criminal investigation.
“The subpoenas are real. The search warrants are real. The investigations are real,” D’Esposito said, adding that the investigation would pursue allegations of fraud, exploitation and trafficking.
The administration is also investigating nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, over allegations involving international students and US wages. Labour Department officials said subpoenas had already been served in those investigations.
The latest action places some of the world's largest IT outsourcing firms, including several major Indian companies, under heightened scrutiny as Washington moves to tighten enforcement of US foreign-labour rules.

sources.news_title: Trump admin bars Microsoft and other tech companies from seeking permanent residency for foreign workers
sources.text:
(CNN) — The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft and some other companies from seeking permanent residency for foreign workers hired through the H-1B visa program, accusing them of taking advantage of the process so that they could replace American citizens with cheaper labor from abroad.
Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the tech giant is one of a handful of companies to be barred indefinitely from the Labor Department’s PERM program following an investigation spearheaded by the anti-fraud task force that he chairs.
That probe determined that Microsoft laid off roughly 6,000 American workers last year, while at the same time employing 6,300 non-citizens that it had brought to the US by obtaining H-1B visas for them.
“The H-1B visa is how the people get into the United States in the first place, and then a PERM program is how those employees stay,” Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft.”
Vance and other top administration officials alleged that Microsoft had misrepresented its needs in applying for permanent residency for its foreign workers, arguing that the program is meant only for workers with “hyper-specialized” skill sets that can’t be easily found in the US.
Instead, they accused the company of using the program primarily to replace skilled American employees with similarly qualified immigrants who it could pay less to do the same job.
“The fraud is that they’re making representations when applying for this program that are fundamentally illegitimate and therefore ultimately illegal,” Vance said.
In a post on its website, Microsoft officials disputed Vance’s assertions, saying that 80% of the roughly 6,000 H-1B visa applications the company submitted in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees — not to hire new ones. The rest of its applications were for people hired by the company who were already legally in the US.
“We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings,” Microsoft officials wrote. “We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.”
The announcement also raised immediate questions about the timing of the administration’s targeting of Microsoft. In a separate ceremony on Thursday, President Donald Trump is due to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
The medal is the nation’s highest honor for technological achievement and is awarded to those who make “outstanding contributions to America’s economic, environmental and social well-being,” according to the US Patent and Trademark Office.
Vance downplayed the administration’s decision to punish Microsoft over accusations of fraud on the same day that it hailed the company’s achievements.
“Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company, it’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans,” he said. “So we’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.”
The Labor Department is also indefinitely suspending software firm Adobe and several IT outsourcing firms from the PERM program, meaning that any new or pending requests for permanent residency for their workers will not be considered.
Vance did not lay out any specific steps for the companies to regain access to the process, saying only that it wanted Microsoft and others to “change their behavior, improve their behavior and actually get better.”
The move marks the Trump administration’s latest attempt to show it’s cracking down on instances of government “fraud” ahead of the midterm elections, framing the issue as critical to ensuring Americans have fair access to job opportunities and federal benefits.
Trump officials on Thursday also announced that they planned to separately investigate several universities over allegations of that they had abused the J-1 visa program, which allows them to bring in foreign nationals as students, researchers or teachers.
Under that program, Vance said, officials believe that schools regularly employ workers from abroad as a way to undercut the salaries that they would otherwise need to pay to Americans in those positions.
The universities under scrutiny are Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; California Institute of Technology; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; and Arizona State University.
This story was updated with additional information.

US Vice-President JD Vance announced the action alongside Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, who said the companies affected include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. Sonderling said: "I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world — Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini."
The PERM programme is administered by the US Department of Labor.
It generally requires an employer sponsoring a foreign worker for permanent residence to show that there are not sufficient qualified US workers available for the job and that employing the foreign worker will not adversely affect wages and working conditions.
PERM is one of the main stages before an employer can proceed with an employment-based green card application.
The action does not mean that employees of the affected companies automatically lose their H-1B visas or existing green cards.
Instead, it affects the companies’ ability to use the PERM process for employment-based permanent residency. It could therefore delay green card applications for foreign workers whose employers have not yet completed the labor-certification stage.
Notably, the announcement is part of a wider crackdown by the Donald Trump administration on employment-based immigration.
Vance accused companies of using H-1B workers to replace American employees and said the programme had become "rife with fraud".
The Vice President specifically criticised Microsoft, saying: "The message to Microsoft is you’ve got to hire American workers."

Indian technology companies are particularly affected because Indian nationals account for a large share of H-1B workers, while firms such as TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL and Cognizant have historically been significant users of the US employment-visa system.

sources.news_title: U.S. suspends Microsoft, major IT firms from key green card program
sources.text: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration froze on Thursday some green-card filings by Microsoft, Adobe and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine top universities, widening a visa crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs. The twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs — potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers — while putting some of the country’s top research universities on notice. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” Vice President JD Vance said. He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. The announcement about the permanent labor certification process — PERM — came hours before Trump was due to give Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. Under PERM, required for most employment-based green cards, employers must show that hiring a foreign worker will not harm U.S. workers’ wages or job opportunities. Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, according to data from the US labor department. The company said in a statement that about 80 per cent of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers. In July, the company said it would cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1 per cent of its global workforce. U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said. He said these companies had since 2009 sought almost three million foreign workers, and had received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to U.S. immigration data. Vance said the suspensions would last “as long as it needs to,” adding that the administration wants the companies to change how they hire. He said some companies post ineffective job ads, then cite a lack of applicants to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers. Microsoft said in its statement that it pays its H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work. “The immediate financial impact on major technology companies may be relatively limited at this moment, but the longer-term implications for innovation and competitiveness could be much more significant,” said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment. Nasscom, India’s IT industry body, said Indian tech companies in the US had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, and relatively few of their workers sought green cards through the PERM process. Crackdown widens The suspensions are the latest in a series of steps against skilled-worker programs. In September last year, the U.S. Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called “Project Firewall” as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time US$100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad. During President Donald Trump’s second term, companies have faced growing pressure to keep jobs and production in the United States rather than move them overseas. The action comes despite closer ties between the administration and tech leaders, who are lobbying for lighter AI regulation. Universities under scrutiny Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages. The nine schools also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Labor Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas had already been served. D’Esposito said investigators would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa abuse were compromising federally funded research. “It could have an enormous economic impact on the whole US economy,” said Sarah Spreitzer, a vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents. International students historically spent US$40 billion a year while in the US, she said. The probe deepens the administration’s long-running fight with Harvard over foreign students. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed the university over alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with immigration law. Harvard called that subpoena “unfounded retribution” but said it would comply as far as the law requires. --- Reporting by Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff, Doina Chiacu in Washington and Prathik Jayaprakash in Bengaluru; Editing by Mark Porter, Sayantani Ghosh and Sanjeev Miglani

It’s unclear why the Trump administration is targeting the Redmond, Wash., based company, but Vance accused Microsoft of being the most frequent hirer of foreign workers over American applicants.
The VP claimed the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while receiving 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“Our message to Microsoft is: you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants,” said Vance, pointing out that overseas workers are subject to deportation if they lose their job.

sources.news_title: US suspends Infosys, Microsoft, Wipro, HCL, Cognizant, Adobe, 2 other IT firms from labour programme: Here’s why
sources.text:
The Trump administration on Thursday suspended several major technology companies, including Microsoft, Infosys, Cognizant, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Capgemini and Adobe, from the US Permanent Labour Certification Programme (PERM), accusing companies of abusing the system used to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency.
US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the move alongside Vice President JD Vance and the head of the US Anti-Fraud Task Force at a briefing in Washington.
Sonderling said the Department of Labour would stop accepting new applications under PERM, a green card program that allows skilled foreign workers to gain permanent residency through their employment, and processing pending permanent labour certification applications involving the companies.
Quick answers to key questions
The companies named were Microsoft, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant, Tata, Capgemini and Adobe.
PERM allows employers to seek labour certification to sponsor eligible foreign workers for employment-based permanent residency, including some workers who entered through the H-1B programme.
The administration accused the companies of making allegedly illegitimate representations in their applications and abusing the system. The companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The Department of Labour said it would stop accepting new applications and processing pending PERM applications involving the companies. This could affect some employees’ green-card applications.
Vice President JD Vance said the suspensions would be indefinite, suggesting they would remain in place until the administration’s concerns were addressed.
“I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini,” Sonderling said.
He added that Microsoft and Adobe would also be suspended from the programme.
Vance accused the companies of making allegedly illegitimate representations when applying for the labour certification programme.
“The fraud is that they’re making representations when applying for this program that are fundamentally illegitimate and therefore ultimately illegal,” Vance said.
The vice president specifically singled out Microsoft, saying no US company had “abused this system more” than the software giant.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said.
He urged the affected companies to change their hiring practices and employ more US workers.
“Stop defrauding the American worker. Stop importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do,” Vance said.
“Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them, they do a lot of important things,” he said. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company. It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.”
Vance said the suspensions would be indefinite, suggesting that the companies would remain barred from the programme until the Trump administration's concerns were addressed.
Sonderling also said multiple active federal investigations were underway in connection with the issue.
The Permanent Labour Certification Programme, commonly known as PERM, allows US employers to seek certification to sponsor eligible foreign workers for employment-based permanent residency, including workers who may have entered the country through the H-1B visa programme.
The latest action could therefore affect the ability of the named companies to advance certain green-card applications for foreign employees.
Sonderling said the companies targeted by the administration had collectively sought nearly three million foreign workers since 2009.
“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications,” he said.
Sonderling argued that the scale of foreign-worker hiring had come at the expense of American employees.
“That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” he said.
The companies named by the administration did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The suspension is the latest move by the Trump administration targeting both legal and undocumented immigration pathways.
The technology industry’s reliance on foreign workers, particularly through the H-1B visa system, has become a major point of contention in the US immigration debate.
The administration and its allies have pressed technology companies to train and hire more American workers. Trump has also moved to make the use of H-1B visas more difficult for companies seeking to recruit foreign talent.

sources.news_title: H-1B Shock For Indians: Infosys, Wipro, HCL Among Firms Hit By US Green Card Suspension
sources.text:
H-1B Shock For Indians: Infosys, Wipro, HCL Among Firms Hit By US Green Card Suspension | Explained
In the latest development, the United States has taken fresh action against the use of foreign labour programmes, with the administration suspending major technology companies from the PERM (Program Electronic Review Management) labour certification programme, a key step in the process of obtaining employment-based green cards for foreign workers.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
US Vice President JD Vance announced the suspension involving Microsoft on Thursday, accusing the company of misusing the system and arguing that American companies should give greater priority to US workers.
The US Department of Labor has also been investigating alleged fraud and abuse linked to the H-1B and PERM systems. The department's inspector general said in July that investigators were looking into schemes involving fraudulent applications and the exploitation of foreign workers.
Reports said the latest action also covers technology companies including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini and Adobe.
What Is The PERM Programme?
PERM stands for Program Electronic Review Management. It is a US Department of Labor process generally used by employers that want to sponsor certain foreign workers for permanent employment in the United States.
Before an employer can move ahead with many employment-based green-card applications, it generally needs labour certification from the Department of Labor.
The process is designed to establish that there are not enough qualified and willing US workers available for the particular job and that employing the foreign worker will not negatively affect the wages and working conditions of US workers.
The Department of Labor continues to maintain PERM as part of its Foreign Labor Certification programmes.
Why Has The US Taken Action?
The Trump administration has stepped up scrutiny of programmes used to employ foreign workers.
Vance said the action against Microsoft followed an ongoing investigation. He argued that companies benefiting from the US economy should also make greater efforts to employ American workers.
According to the Associated Press, Vance said Microsoft would no longer be able to use the PERM route to take H-1B workers through the permanent-residency process while the suspension remains in place.
The administration has accused some companies and labour intermediaries of using immigration programmes in ways that could disadvantage American workers. These remain allegations connected to ongoing investigations, rather than findings of guilt against every company named in reports.
What Does This Mean For H-1B Workers?
The development is important for H-1B workers because many foreign professionals use H-1B status as a temporary work route before their employers seek permanent residency for them.
However, a PERM suspension is not the same as cancelling H-1B visas.
The immediate impact is mainly on the employer's ability to start or continue the relevant labour-certification process for new green-card cases.
For workers who have already moved further ahead in the green-card process, the impact can be different depending on the stage of their case. For example, a suspension of new PERM filings does not automatically mean that every existing green-card case or H-1B status is cancelled.
Why Indian IT Workers Are Watching The Move
The action has particular importance for Indian technology professionals because Indian IT companies are major participants in the US technology and immigration ecosystem.
Companies such as TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL and Cognizant have historically had large numbers of employees working in the US.
The Department of Labor's own historical PERM data shows the significant role played by major technology companies, including Cognizant, Microsoft, Infosys, Wipro and HCL America, in employment-based labour certification.
Earlier this year, Cognizant separately became the subject of a PERM suspension amid a federal investigation into alleged visa-related fraud. The action stopped the company from filing new PERM applications while the investigation continued.
Does This Mean H-1B Visas Are Being Stopped?
No. The two programmes serve different purposes.
The H-1B programme allows US employers to employ foreign workers in certain specialised occupations on a temporary basis.
The PERM process, in contrast, is connected to the permanent employment and green-card process.
Therefore, an employee affected by a PERM suspension is not automatically losing their H-1B visa or their right to work in the US.
The exact effect will depend on the company involved and the stage of the worker's immigration case.
US Administration Says American Workers Must Come First
The latest action is part of a wider push by the Trump administration to tighten oversight of foreign-worker programmes.
The Department of Labor's inspector general said in July that the agency had launched a major investigation into alleged H-1B and PERM fraud, including claims of fraudulent applications, worker exploitation and practices that could undercut American workers.
The administration says stronger enforcement is needed to protect US workers and prevent companies from abusing immigration programmes.
At the same time, the impact on foreign professionals, particularly workers from India who are waiting for employer-sponsored permanent residency, could be significant if similar actions expand to more companies.
What's NEXT?
The companies affected by the latest action could face delays in starting or progressing certain employment-based green-card cases while investigations continue.
The Department of Labor is already processing a large PERM workload. Its latest processing data showed applications from June 2026 were still in the processing queue, with the average analyst-review time for August cases at 336 calendar days.

The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from a federal program that companies use to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said Thursday during a press conference.
Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM. The program is an initial step that employers generally must complete before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based green card, requiring them to show that no qualified and available US workers could fill the role.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.
Microsoft filed more certified PERM applications than any other employer in the first three quarters of this fiscal year, with 1504, according to a Business Insider analysis, and an additional 174 were filed for subsidiaries LinkedIn and Activision. Adobe filed 168 in the same time period.
The announcement came just over a week after Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella sat two seats away from Vance at President Donald Trump's White House "Super Intelligence" luncheon, a gathering of tech executives focused on AI.
A Microsoft spokesperson pointed Business Insider to a blog post the company published Thursday, which said “the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans.”
Microsoft wrote that roughly 80% of the about 6,000 H-1B visa applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees, rather than to hire new people. It said the remaining applications were for people already legally in the US and amounted to 1% of its US workforce.
Adobe did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the administration was also suspending Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini from the program. The IT companies are among the largest users of PERM and other employment-based immigration pathways in the US.
Vance also said the administration would investigate nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, and Stanford, over allegations that they used J-1 exchange visas to undercut American wages. Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.
The announcement is the latest escalation for the administration against companies that rely on highly skilled foreign workers, particularly through the H-1B visa system. Microsoft is one of the biggest employers of H-1B workers in the US.
It was not immediately clear how long the suspension would last or what it would mean for Microsoft employees whose permanent-residency cases are already pending. The process is already slow: The Labor Department says PERM applications took an average of 336 calendar days to process in August.

sources.news_title: U.S. suspends Microsoft, Adobe from green-card labor program in foreign worker crackdown
sources.text:
The U.S. Department of Labor announced it would suspend Microsoft and Adobe from its Permanent Labor Certification program on Thursday, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said, as the Trump administration continues to take aim at immigration and foreign hiring programs ahead of November's midterm elections.
Sonderling said the Labor Department won't accept or process any new applications under the program for a host of companies, including Cognizant, Infosys, Capgemini, Tata, Wipro and HCL.
The secretary said Adobe and Microsoft were also suspended "due to multiple active federal investigations."
"Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers," Sonderling said.
Vice President JD Vance criticized Microsoft specifically, pointing to the firm's 6,000 layoffs in 2025. Vance claimed that the company "replaced" those workers with people on H-1B visas.
"So we're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we're also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first," Vance said.
Microsoft responded to Vance's claims and defended its hiring practices in a statement Thursday, saying "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans."
"Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees," the company said.
President Donald Trump is set to award the National Medal of Science to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other leading technology CEOs on Thursday at the same summit where the suspension announcement was made.
Nadella is from India and moved to the U.S. in 1988. He joined Microsoft in 1992.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su are also being honored at Thursday's medal ceremony. Each of the leaders immigrated to the U.S. Musk was born in South Africa and Su and Huang were born in Taiwan.
"It's one thing if you want to bring in a person like Elon Musk," Vance said. "I think 99% of American citizens look at somebody like Elon Musk or Lisa Su, the CEO of AMD, and they say, obviously, if that person wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America, we support that."
Tech giants like Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Apple have been among the top sponsors of H-1B visas for decades. This year, Amazon had the highest number of petitions at 35,426 workers, followed by Cognizant and EY, according to 2026 data from Levels.fyi.
Microsoft was a close fourth at 21,706 petitions for 2026, with a median base salary of $180,710.
Microsoft said that petitions were only filed for workers "who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and said Microsoft's wages for H-1B workers were among the highest of all H-1B filings.
CNBC has reached out to Adobe for comment.

sources.text:
The US is suspending eight technology firms from PERM, the labour certification step that precedes an employer-sponsored green card, citing alleged fraud. Capgemini is the only European company named, and North America is its fastest-growing region at 29% of group revenue.
The US has suspended eight technology companies from the programme that lets employers sponsor foreign staff for permanent residency. JD Vance announced it on Thursday, citing alleged fraud. One of the eight is European.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling named Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini alongside Microsoft and Adobe, at a White House press conference reported by Reuters. Labor Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas had been served. Microsoft did not immediately respond to Reuters.
What is suspended matters. PERM is the labour certification an employer must obtain before petitioning for a worker’s green card, and the department can hold applications under 20 CFR 656.31 until an investigation finishes.
It covers new filings.
Cases already filed or approved are not cancelled by it, and nobody’s current visa status changes. The wider squeeze is elsewhere, in the $103,265 fee the Department of Homeland Security proposed in August for each new capped H-1B.
This is not the first suspension.
The department’s inspector general opened a nationwide H-1B and PERM fraud investigation in July, citing fraudulent applications, wage kickbacks and benching, then held new filings from Cognizant and the data firm Cloudera in September. Separately, the Justice Department took $3.2M from OpenAI in August over how it advertised PERM roles. No criminal charges have been brought in the labour investigation.
Capgemini is the European name on the list.
The Paris company employs 421,000 people and took EUR 1,721M from North America in the first quarter, a region worth 29% of group revenue and growing faster than any other. It is one of four consultancies in OpenAI’s Frontier Alliances, alongside Accenture, McKinsey and BCG.
Nine universities are also under investigation.
Harvard, Yale and Stanford are among them, accused of bringing in international students to undercut American wages. Subpoenas have already been served there too.
Capgemini spends a good deal of time telling European companies to measure exactly this kind of exposure.
Its research institute found last month that 86% of large organisations have significant exposure to foreign or externally controlled supply chains, and that 36% would need more than a year to leave a critical provider. Its own American green card pipeline has now been suspended with no published end date.

sources.text:
US suspends Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL, other IT firms from Green Card programme
The US Labour Department suspended major IT and outsourcing firms, including Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL, from a programme used by employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency, alleging abuse of the system. Microsoft and Adobe were also suspended amid federal investigations, while nine universities face probes over allegations of undercutting American wages.
The US Department of Labour has suspended some of the world’s largest IT outsourcing firms, including Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL, from the Permanent Labour Certification Program (PERM), accusing companies of abusing the system for foreign workers seeking permanent residency.
PERM is a labour certification that employers typically need before sponsoring a foreign worker for an employment-based Green Card. It is required for several major employment-based Green Card categories, although not all of them.
Under the programme, employers must demonstrate to the US Department of Labour that there are no qualified, willing and available US workers for a specific job, and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.
WHY DOES IT MATTER?
The move puts pressure on Indian IT firms such as Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL, which are major employers of Indian professionals in the US, and could affect employees seeking to transition from temporary work status to permanent residency.
However, the action does not cancel H-1B visas or prevent these companies from employing H-1B workers. Instead, the suspension blocks the companies from filing new PERM applications and puts pending applications on hold for as long as the suspension remains in effect. The Indian IT firms could also face higher legal, compliance and administrative costs.
“So, what do the new measures mean?” US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling asked, before adding: “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certifications involving these companies.”
WHY MICROSOFT IS AT THE CENTRE OF THE ACTION
Thanking US President Donald Trump, Sonderling announced the action against Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini, while also suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the programme, citing multiple active federal investigations.
He said the move amounted to “cutting off the head of the snake” at the heart of “stealing jobs from capable Americans”.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Sonderling said at a White House press conference, with US Vice President JD Vance by his side.
Vance said Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visa approvals and nearly 3,000 green cards. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indenture."
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” the US Vice President went on to say.
He further said the H-1B visa programme was intended to allow companies to bring in “the best of the best” from outside the US for positions that could not be filled by American workers, but alleged that the programme had become “rife with fraud.”
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft," he added.
However, the crackdown was not just limited to companies. The Labour Department's action also extends to nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, which Sonderling said would be investigated over allegations that they brought in international students to undercut American wages.
Labour Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.
WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR INDIAN IT WORKERS?
The immediate impact for Indian professionals is likely to be delays in the employer-sponsored Green Card process, rather than cancellation of their existing H-1B visas.
Employees of affected companies who are already in the PERM process could see their applications delayed for as long as the suspension remains in place. Those whose employers were preparing to begin the process could also have to wait before new applications can be filed.
This latest move by the Donald Trump administration could have a particular impact on Indian professionals in the US, with about 37% of Indians who obtained Green Cards in FY2023 doing so through employment-based preferences -- a route in which PERM is an important step.
Any prolonged suspension could therefore add to the uncertainty for Indian technology professionals whose employers are sponsoring them for permanent residency.
