sources.news_title: Microsoft is being suspended from program to apply for green cards for skilled foreign workers, Vance says
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is suspending tech giant Microsoft from a program to apply for green cards for workers who come to the U.S. to live and work using H-1B visas as it accuses the company of fraud.
Supporters of Republican President Donald Trump have long argued that various programs like the one Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing essentially empower American companies to recruit foreign workers for jobs that end up undercutting Americans. In a wide-ranging announcement Thursday, Vance and other top administration officials also called out universities over their use of J-1 visas for international students and information technology outsourcing firms.
The announcement came hours before Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, part of an event at which he is granting some of the nation’s most prestigious science and technology awards to his tech billionaire allies.
Vance said that the program from which Microsoft is being suspended requires companies to advertise jobs in America before applying to the Department of Labor to show they need to give a foreign worker a green card because of a lack of American workers.
“They’ll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that ‘We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.’ And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft.”
Vance said Microsoft last year laid off 6,000 American workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said in a White House news conference announcing the decision. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”
Microsoft, which is based in Redmond, Washington, near Seattle, said in a statement that “the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans.”
“We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information,” the statement continued, adding that 80% of the 6,000 H-1B visa applications it submitted in the last fiscal year, were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees, not to hire new personnel.
The remaining filings for new employees were for people “already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” it said.

The Vance announcement came a day after Trump’s administration launched another broadside against international students and their ability to work in the U.S.

US suspends Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL and others from green-card labour programme
- Published OnOct 8, 2026 | 20:35 IST

The US government has suspended Microsoft and several other IT firms, including Adobe and Infosys, from a permanent residency program for skilled foreign workers due to alleged fraud, Vice President JD Vance announced.
The Trump administration has suspended several major technology and IT outsourcing companies, including Microsoft, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Cognizant and Capgemini, from the US Permanent Labour Certification Programme, or PERM, potentially affecting the green-card process for foreign workers.
US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the action alongside Vice President JD Vance and the head of the US Anti-Fraud Task Force, alleging that the companies had misused employment-visa programmes and saying the administration wanted companies to hire more American workers.
Adobe has also been suspended from the programme.
“I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini,” Sonderling said.
He added that the Department of Labour was also suspending Microsoft and Adobe.
The department said it would not accept new or process pending permanent labour certification applications involving the affected companies.
Reuters reported that the administration cited alleged fraud as part of the basis for the action. Vance also alleged that Microsoft had replaced laid-off American workers with foreign employees. Microsoft has not immediately responded to requests for comment, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.
What is the US alleging?
The move comes amid a wider Trump administration crackdown on programmes that allow companies to hire foreign workers.
Vance pointed to Microsoft's layoffs and use of H-1B visas, alleging that the company had replaced American workers with foreign employees.
Sonderling said the companies named by the administration had sought large numbers of foreign workers over the years.
“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They’ve received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications,” he said.
Sonderling alleged that this amounted to hundreds of thousands of jobs being taken from American workers.
The administration's allegations about individual companies and their impact on US workers remain allegations. The immediate action announced by the Labour Department relates to the companies' participation in the PERM programme.
What is PERM?
PERM, or Permanent Labour Certification, is a US Department of Labour process that generally requires an employer to establish that qualified, willing and available US workers cannot be found for a particular job before sponsoring an eligible foreign worker for permanent employment.
The certification is an important step in many employment-based green-card applications. The Labour Department describes permanent labour certification as a process that allows an employer to hire a foreign worker for permanent employment in the US.
The latest suspension therefore affects the employment-based green-card process. It does not automatically cancel an employee's H-1B status.
The distinction is important because H-1B and PERM serve different purposes. H-1B is a temporary work status for specialised occupations, while PERM is linked to the process of obtaining permanent employment and, eventually, a green card.
Why Indian IT workers could be affected
The move is particularly significant for Indian technology professionals because companies such as Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL have large US operations and employ workers through the country's skilled-worker immigration system.
Indian professionals are also major beneficiaries of the H-1B programme. According to the Associated Press, technology companies are the biggest users of H-1B visas, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
The crackdown also follows an earlier action against Cognizant. In September, the US suspended the company's PERM filings amid a federal investigation into alleged fraud involving employment-visa programmes.
The latest action brings Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL, along with Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant and Capgemini, under the PERM restrictions announced by the administration.
Does the move suspend H-1B visas?
No. The announcement does not amount to a blanket suspension or cancellation of H-1B visas for employees of the affected companies.
The immediate restriction applies to new and pending PERM labour-certification applications involving the companies named by the administration.
The impact on individual employees will depend on where their employment-based immigration case is in the green-card process.
The PERM action comes as the Trump administration increases scrutiny of foreign-worker and international-student programmes.
The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students participating in the Optional Practical Training programme, according to the Associated Press. OPT allows eligible international students to work in jobs related to their field of study during or after their education in the US.
The Labour Department has also opened investigations involving universities. Reuters reported that nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, are being investigated over allegations involving international students and wages, with subpoenas issued by the department's inspector general.

sources.news_title: US suspending permanent residency program for Microsoft, Vance says
sources.text:
By Akash Sriram and Steve Holland
WASHINGTON, Oct 8 (Reuters) – The US suspended Microsoft, major IT outsourcers and software maker Adobe from a key green-card program on Thursday while opening probes into nine top universities, widening a crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.
Since taking office, US President Donald Trump has pursued a broad effort to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship. Thursday’s twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs — potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers — while putting some of the country’s top research universities on notice.
“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” Vice President JD Vance said. He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
His comments came hours before Trump honored tech billionaires for their contributions to America, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. Nadella once held an H-1B visa, as did Elon Musk, who was also honored, while three of the other CEOs honored are immigrants.
Nadella thanked Trump for the medal, saying in a post on X he would continue to advance technology and drive American prosperity.
Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, or the permanent labor certification process, according to data from the US labor department. Under PERM, which most employment-based green cards require, employers must show a foreign hire will not hurt US workers’ wages or jobs.
The company said in a statement that about 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers. In July, the company said it would cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1% of its global workforce.
CRACKDOWN WIDENS
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.
He said these companies had since 2009 sought almost three million foreign workers, and had received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications.
Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to US immigration data.
Vance said the suspensions would last “as long as it needs to,” and that the administration wanted the companies to change how they hire. He said some companies post ineffective job ads, then point to the lack of applicants to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers.
Microsoft said in its statement that it pays its H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.
Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment.
Nasscom, India’s IT industry body, said Indian tech companies in the US had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, and relatively few of their workers sought green cards through the PERM process.
In September last year, the Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called “Project Firewall” as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad.
UNIVERSITIES UNDER SCRUTINY
Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages.
The nine schools also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Labor Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.
D’Esposito said investigators would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa abuse were compromising federally funded research.
“It could have an enormous economic impact on the whole US economy,” said Sarah Spreitzer, a vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents. International students historically spent $40 billion a year while in the US, she said.
The probe deepens the administration’s long-running fight with Harvard over foreign students. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed the university over alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with immigration law. Harvard called that subpoena “unfounded retribution” but said it would comply as far as the law requires.
Rapidly changing visa policies caused a sharp drop in international applications to Columbia University and contributed to the university pausing admissions to one of its journalism programs, Reuters reported last week.
(Reporting by Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff, Doina Chiacu in Washington, Aditya Soni in New York and Prathik Jayaprakash in Bengaluru; Editing by Mark Porter, Sayantani Ghosh and Sanjeev Miglani)

sources.news_title: Vance Freezes Microsoft’s Green-Card Pipeline, Accuses Software Giant Of Fraud
sources.text:
JD Vance just put one of America’s biggest technology companies on notice: being successful does not earn you a free pass on American jobs.
The Trump administration announced Thursday that Microsoft is being suspended from the federal labor-certification program companies use to sponsor workers for employment-based green cards.
Adobe and six major IT outsourcing firms are also caught in the crackdown.
This is a concrete restriction on the companies’ access to the immigration system, and Vance made clear that he wants a change in hiring practices.
Watch his announcement:
Vice President JD Vance announces the suspension of the PERM Program for Microsoft:
"Thanks to an ongoing investigation, we have decided to suspend the PERM program for Microsoft, which means they will no longer be able to take those H-1Bs and apply for permanent resident status… pic.twitter.com/xMSgLgcqTI
— Vice President JD Vance (@VP) October 8, 2026
The administration puts American workers at the center
As RealClearPolitics reports, Vance connected the suspension to an ongoing investigation and accused companies of making improper representations when seeking access to foreign-worker programs.
Pressed by a reporter to explain the alleged fraud, he argued that businesses cannot legitimately claim they need specialized foreign talent while using the system to replace Americans and drive down wages.
He also said the administration wants the technology industry to succeed and keep investing in the United States. His demand is that American workers benefit from that success, rather than being treated as an expense to eliminate.
That is an important distinction for a company with Microsoft’s influence: support for American technology does not have to mean accepting every hiring practice without scrutiny.
A famous logo should not buy a company an exemption from the rules everyone else has to follow.
Vance cited Microsoft’s layoffs and visa figures in laying out his accusation. Microsoft has since disputed the implication that its applications represented thousands of new foreign hires; its response is below.
BREAKING: VP JD Vance takes aim at Microsoft, accusing the tech giant of laying off thousands of American workers while bringing in foreign workers to replace them through the H-1B visa system.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the… pic.twitter.com/qucLP6IfbT
— Fox News (@FoxNews) October 8, 2026
Eight companies, and a freeze on pending applications
The Lynnwood Times reports that the suspension covers Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department would stop accepting new permanent labor-certification applications from the named companies and stop processing their pending applications. He cited active federal investigations in announcing the action against Microsoft and Adobe.
For businesses that rely on sponsoring workers for permanent residency, that reaches beyond future recruiting plans. It puts an immediate obstacle in front of applications already moving through the system.
The freeze concerns the labor-certification process; it does not automatically cancel existing H-1B visas or mean that every foreign employee at these companies must leave the country. Keeping those distinctions straight matters when an announcement affects real employees and their families.
Here is Sonderling identifying the companies and explaining the action:
.@Sonderling47: "I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world — Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini — and also, due to multiple active federal investigations, @USDOL is suspending… https://t.co/ENyAFHSo93 pic.twitter.com/DZXcRMp22L
— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 8, 2026
What this program is supposed to do
The Department of Labor explains that permanent labor certification, commonly called PERM, is a step most employers must complete before submitting an employment-based immigration petition to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
Labor must determine that enough qualified, willing and available U.S. workers cannot be found for the particular job in the relevant area. It must also determine that hiring the foreign worker will not harm the wages and working conditions of comparable American workers.
In plain English, protecting American workers is already part of the program’s purpose. It is not an extra condition Vance invented at a press conference.
That is why the hiring records matter so much here: the central question is whether the companies met those requirements in the actual jobs and applications under review.
Americans who have lost work deserve more than a corporate slogan about talent shortages. They deserve to know whether they received a genuine chance at the jobs in question.
Microsoft pushes back on the numbers
In its Thursday statement, Microsoft said about 80% of the approximately 6,000 H-1B applications it submitted in the last fiscal year involved extending or changing the status of people it already employed.
The company said the remaining applications for new employees concerned people already legally in the United States, and that those hires equaled about 1% of its U.S. workforce. It also said most of its U.S. employees are Americans.
Microsoft defended its compensation practices, saying H-1B workers receive the same pay as other employees doing comparable work. It said it looks forward to giving the administration additional information.
That response makes a meaningful point about how to read the totals: a visa application is not automatically a new arrival or a one-for-one replacement for a laid-off worker.
It does not, by itself, resolve whether particular labor-certification applications complied with the rules. That requires the underlying records, not competing press statements.
The suspension is real; allegations of fraud still need to be established. Readers should not confuse an announced investigation with a court finding that every company on the list broke the law.
Now comes the test
The administration has put a meaningful tool behind its America First message. The next test is whether investigators can document the alleged abuses and whether the companies change any practices the evidence shows were improper.
Microsoft says its records will tell a different story. Fine: produce them and let the investigation establish what happened.
American workers deserve an immigration system that keeps its promises to them. Even when the company asking for access is Microsoft.

Please share your thoughts about this article below. We value your opinions, and would love to see you add to the discussion!

sources.news_title: US visa chaos: Tata, Wipro among IT firms suspended from PERM scheme; what it means
sources.text:
NEW DELHI: The Trump administration has stepped up its crackdown on the US immigration system, suspending major technology companies including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, Capgemini and HCL from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme amid allegations of abuse of H-1B visas and the employment of foreign workers.
US Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of laying off thousands of American workers while simultaneously benefiting from thousands of H-1B visas and green cards. The administration has also put nine universities under investigation over alleged misuse of visa-related programmes, adding to growing uncertainty for foreign workers and international students in the US.
Announcing Microsoft's suspension from the PERM programme, Vance said the company had laid off 6,000 American workers while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft."
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said at a White House news conference.
Vance also accused companies of using foreign workers to undercut American employees, saying: "This is a fundamental INSULT to the American worker and to the American way of life. We CANNOT allow visa programs that were designed to ensure that American corporations had access to the best and the brightest, to use them to undercut the wages of American workers!"
What is the PERM programme
The Permanent Labour Certification programme, or PERM, is a Department of Labour process that allows US employers to seek certification to permanently employ foreign workers.
Under the process, employers generally have to demonstrate that there are not enough able, willing, qualified and available US workers for the job and that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed American workers.
Once the labour certification is approved by the Department of Labour, the employer can proceed with an immigrant petition to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, generally through Form I-140.
For H-1B workers, PERM can therefore form an important step in the employment-based green card process. Suspending a company's access to the programme can make it harder for the company to sponsor eligible foreign workers for permanent residence.
How PERM was meant to protect US workers
The PERM programme is designed to ensure that American workers are not disadvantaged when employers seek to hire foreign workers for permanent jobs. Before sponsoring a foreign worker for a green card, an employer generally has to demonstrate that there are not enough qualified, willing and available US workers for the position and that hiring the foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed Americans.
The concern for US authorities arises when employers manipulate or bypass this labour-market test. Fraudulent recruitment can make it appear that no suitable American worker is available when, in reality, qualified US workers may have been discouraged from applying or effectively excluded from consideration. The Department of Labor's inspector general has identified vulnerabilities in the PERM system, including concerns over fraudulent applications, inadequate supporting documentation and weaknesses in post-certification enforcement.
Wages are another concern. Employers are required to meet prevailing wage requirements, which are intended to prevent foreign-worker hiring from depressing wages for American workers in comparable jobs. If employers circumvent these requirements or use arrangements that effectively reduce the foreign worker's compensation, the government says the system can undermine the safeguards built into PERM.
The administration's latest moves have also extended beyond companies. The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a $70,000 fee for international students participating in the Optional Practical Training programme, which allows eligible foreign students to work in jobs related to their studies.

Microsoft is No. 5 among US employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No. 1.
Vance said Microsoft last year laid off 6,000 American workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.

Vance said H-1B workers are effectively foreign indentured servants because if they lose their jobs, they have to leave the country, and they earn less than Americans in the same position.
Microsoft, which is based in Redmond, Washington, said of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications it submitted in the last fiscal year, 80 percent were “to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
“These were not to hire new people,” Microsoft said in a statement. “The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country.”
The company added that it only files H-1B petitions for “those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category.”
Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at USCIS during the Biden administration, called Vance’s announcement “incoherent.”
“If the Trump administration were truly concerned that H-1B workers are ‘indentured servants,’ then the last thing they would do is block companies from helping their own H-1B workers get green cards,” he said. “Once you have a green card, you’re no longer dependent on your employer for your immigration status — you’re a permanent resident who can change jobs and negotiate higher wages without fear.”
H-1B program has been scrutinized
The H-1B program has long been a target of Trump supporters who say that the program undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.

Ron Hira, a Howard University political science professor and longtime critic of the H-1B program, called the move against Microsoft “very significant.’’ Hira noted the White House last month issued a little-noticed executive order directing government agencies to “implement appropriate measures to protect American workers from abuse of the H-1B program and ensure that the program serves the national interest.’’
“There are supposed to be protections for US workers that say: If you hire an H-1B, you are promising that you are not adversely affecting similarly employed US workers,’’ Hira said. “That’s never been enforced.’’

Vance singled out nine universities that he said merited further investigation for J-1 visa fraud, saying they used the program in greater proportions than their counterparts.
The universities were Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; the California Institute of Technology; Arizona State; and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Stanford said it would cooperate with the investigation.
MIT and Brown said they had received and were reviewing subpoenas from the government related to programs for foreign workers.
“Of note, each J-1 visa holder at MIT has been vetted and authorized to come here by the U.S. government, and we take seriously our obligations to follow U.S. law,” MIT spokesperson Kimberly Allen said in a written statement.
Associated Press writers Heather Hollingsworth in Mission, Kansas, Kelvin Chan in London and Paul Wiseman, Annie Ma and Collin Binkley in Washington contributed. Ortutay reported from Oakland, Calif.

sources.news_title: Green card update: Trump admin blocks tech companies from H-1B PERM program
sources.text:
The Trump administration blocked multiple tech companies, including Microsoft and Adobe, from applying for green cards for their H-1B visa holders Thursday, saying they would no longer steal jobs from American workers.
In an announcement led by Vice President JD Vance, officials said companies seen as using the green card pathway to hire cheap labor and undercut American workers would have their access to the PERM program suspended.
Vance used Microsoft as a key example of the alleged abuse, noting that the tech giant laid off thousands of workers in the past year while still applying for H-1B visas and subsequent green cards.
"Now, our message to Microsoft and to any other foreign or domestic corporation is quite simple: We obviously want you to thrive in the United States of America," Vance said.
"We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector. We are the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers," Vance said. "And so, our message to Microsoft is you're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers."
Microsoft responded to the announcement, saying in a statement shared with Newsweek that it believes in the "strength and talent of the American workforce."
"That is why the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans," the statement read.
"Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category. We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work."
The announcement sparked praise from some immigration reform advocacy groups, and some pushback, including from the libertarian Cato Institute.
"This is further evidence of the Trump administration's lawless antipathy to high-skilled legal immigrants," David Bier, Cato's director of immigration studies, told Newsweek. "The Department of Labor cannot legally suspend a company that it has not proven has violated the rules. As far as I know, they haven't yet detailed exactly what they are doing here, but this policy would have extremely negative effects on workers and companies.
"The companies cannot expand their operations in the United States if they don't know who they can hire or not, and the workers may be forced to leave the United States if the companies cannot sponsor them for green cards when their H-1B visas expire."
Jeremy Beck, co-president of the immigration reform group NumbersUSA, told Newsweek Vance's announcement was significant as no sitting vice president had "ever acknowledged what millions of Americans have come to know: the H-1B visa program displaces Americans and exploits guest workers."
"Bully for Vance and his team for making an example of an American company," Beck said.
Microsoft, Adobe Among Tech Companies Suspended
While Vance focused on Microsoft in his speech, the Department of Labor (DOL) also suspended other major tech companies from the PERM process Thursday.
U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said IT outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini would all be suspended from the program. Adobe and Microsoft's suspensions were due to "multiple active federal investigations," Sonderling said.
The secretary said this meant current green card applications would not be processed further and no new applications would be accepted from the affected companies.
During the White House announcement, Vance said that no company had abused the H-1B program and its green card pathway more than Microsoft.
"So, in the last year, Microsoft—and I want to be clear about the data here…Microsoft laid off last year 6,000 American workers," Vance said. "At the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
"In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replace that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants."
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) figures show Microsoft received 6,258 H-1B approvals in the last fiscal year, while Department of Labor numbers show 3,157 PERM filings.
Microsoft said in its statement that it would look to provide the administration with more details on how it uses the program.
"Microsoft succeeds as a global technology leader by developing the world’s best technology workforce," the company's statement read. "We do this by strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world."
Doug Rand, a former DHS official, said in a statement shared with Newsweek that the administration's actions may not help the situation it is trying to address.
"If the Trump administration were truly concerned that H-1B workers are 'indentured servants,' then the last thing they would do is block companies from helping their own H-1B workers get green cards," Rand said. "Once you have a green card, you're no longer dependent on your employer for your immigration status—you're a permanent resident who can change jobs and negotiate higher wages without fear."
Newsweek reached out to all affected companies for comment via email.
What Is the PERM Program?
The PERM program is the system the DOL uses to issue what is known as Permanent Labor Certification.
While not unique to the H-1B, it is commonly associated with the high-skilled work visa, which has a two-term limit of six years. After that time, companies can opt to apply for a green card for that immigrant worker.
Unlike the initial H-1B process, employers have to prove to the government that the visa holder is the only person suitable for the role linked to their green card application, and that efforts have been made to find an American-born worker to fill that job.
Part of the issue for critics of the program is that companies can simply advertise the role in a Sunday newspaper, and if no one else applies, this can be taken as evidence of an exhaustive search.
Advocates of the PERM process argue it gives employers stability, as well as stability to H-1B workers who may have moved to the U.S. with a spouse and/or children, whose lives would also be uprooted if permanent residency is not an option.
Trump Admin Cites Fraud, Loss of American Jobs
Sonderling, Vance, and other administration officials laid out the issues they see with the H-1B-to-green-card pipeline, raising long-running concerns about potential fraud and the displacement of American-born workers.
The Labor secretary said that while his department had uncovered $22 billion in visa fraud, what was being announced Thursday was more valuable than that—limiting fraud that had "flooded our country with foreign labor" at the expense of U.S. workers.
"The fraud doesn't end with getting the job," he said. "That job becomes a pathway for foreign workers and their families to stay in America permanently and eventually becoming U.S. citizens. And who pays for all that? American workers."
Sonderling said companies had for too long been allowed to bring in cheaper labor through the H-1B program, and that the administration was actively investigating those bending immigration rules to do so.
Advocates have argued that H-1B visas are necessary because there are not enough American-born workers who are skilled enough or willing and able to fill certain roles.
Vance said it was insulting to suggest that Americans would not work on farms, in certain "dirty jobs," or in business and technology, adding that it was a lie that Americans were not good enough to build the future of the country.
Earlier, however, Vance said the high-skilled visa program had some positives, pointing to Elon Musk as an example of someone who had benefited the United States.
Vance Questioned on Microsoft CEO Honor
Vance's first question after the speeches concerned a ceremony at the White House later Thursday involving tech leaders and President Donald Trump.
The president is set to present medals to executives including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, whose company has now been barred from the PERM program.
"Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them. They do a lot of important things," Vance said, before again pointing to the layoffs. "Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company, it's that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans."
Other tech executives set to be honored include Musk, Dell Computers' Michael Dell, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Vance Calls for H-1B Reform
While Vance remained largely skeptical of the H-1B program, he did not call for it to be scrapped. Instead, he said reform was needed.
"This is a terribly pernicious system. It's gone on for too long, and we'd all encourage, by the way, Congress do something about it," Vance said, adding later, "It is very clear it's not working in the way that it should."
Beck agreed, pointing to attempts by lawmakers to reform the visa that have so far failed to pass.
"Today’s announcement won’t end the financial incentive to displace Americans with cheaper, captive foreign-workers. That takes reforms that only Congress can pass: limiting the program to genuine shortages and requiring wages high enough that no employer would choose a guest worker just to save money," Beck said. "Those reforms would treat guest workers more fairly, too."
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Sam Wilson.

sources.news_title: Vance says Microsoft is being suspended from program to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers
sources.text:
By SEUNG MIN KIM and REBECCA SANTANA
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration announced Thursday it was suspending Microsoft and several other firms from a program allowing foreign workers to apply for green cards as it also lashed out at universities that bring international students to the U.S. on exchange programs.
The announcement by Vice President JD Vance marks the latest swing from the Trump administration at employers and universities that welcome foreign students and workers into the country.
Such programs have frequently been targeted by some Trump supporters who argue they undercut American students and workers. Supporters say they allow the U.S. to attract the best talent from around the world and fill important hiring gaps.
Supporters of the Republican president have long argued that various programs like H-1B visas — which Vance accused Microsoft of abusing — essentially empower American companies to recruit foreign workers for jobs that end up undercutting Americans. In the wide-ranging announcement, Vance and other top administration officials also called out universities over their use of J-1 visas for international students and information technology outsourcing firms.
The announcement came hours before Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, part of an event at which he is granting some of the nation’s most prestigious science and technology awards to his tech billionaire allies.
Vance says US workers are replaced with ‘foreign indentured servants’
Vance said the program from which Microsoft is being suspended requires companies to advertise jobs in America before applying to the Department of Labor to show they need to give a foreign worker a green card because of a lack of American workers.
“They’ll put an advertisement in a small-town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that ‘We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.’ And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft.”
Microsoft is No. 5 among U.S. employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according data from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No. 1.
Microsoft, which is based in Redmond, Washington, said it looks forward to “providing the Administration with additional information.” Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications it submitted in the last fiscal year, the company said 80% were “to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
“These were not to hire new people,” Microsoft said in a statement. “The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country.”
The company added that it only files H-1B petitions for “those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category.”
Doug Rand, a former senior adviser at USCIS during the Biden administration, called Vance’s announcement “incoherent.”
“If the Trump administration were truly concerned that H-1B workers are ‘indentured servants,’ then the last thing they would do is block companies from helping their own H-1B workers get green cards,” he said. “Once you have a green card, you’re no longer dependent on your employer for your immigration status — you’re a permanent resident who can change jobs and negotiate higher wages without fear.”
Vance said Microsoft last year laid off 6,000 American workers but also obtained 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said in a White House news conference announcing the decision. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”
Vance said H-1B workers are effectively foreign indentured servants because if they lose their job, they have to leave the country, and they earn less than Americans in the same position.
H-1B program has been scrutinized
The H-1B program has long been a target of Trump supporters who say that the program undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.
H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find American workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
Trump last year attempted to ratchet up the fee for H-1B work visas to $100,000, saying it would protect American workers from losing their jobs to lower-paid foreigners, but a federal judge struck that down in June.
The administration has since tried a different tack, announcing plans in August for a $103,265 fee. The proposed regulation described the new fee as a “dedicated revenue mechanism to help recover a portion of the federal government’s costs of administering the lawful immigration system.” The rule isn’t yet final and is expected to face a legal challenge, like the one before it.
Ron Hira, a Howard University political science professor and longtime critic of the H-1B program, called the move against Microsoft “very significant.’’ Hira noted the White House last month issued a little-noticed executive order directing government agencies to “implement appropriate measures to protect American workers from abuse of the H-1B program and ensure that the program serves the national interest.’’
“There are supposed to be protections for U.S. workers that say: If you hire an H-1B, you are promising that you are not adversely affecting similarly employed U.S. workers,’’ Hira said. “That’s never been enforced.’’
Besides Microsoft, Vance said the government was similarly suspending Adobe and tech consulting firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. The companies did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.
Trump also has targeted foreign students
The Vance announcement came a day after Trump’s administration launched another broadside against international students and their ability to work in the U.S.
The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States. The proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the Optional Practical Training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school.
Vance also called out universities, suggesting that they were abusing a program to allow international students to come to the U.S. These temporary visas, called J-1 visas, allow international visitors to temporarily come to the U.S. for work and study exchange programs. In most cases, to get the visa, students must receive the majority of their funding from an institution, such as a fellowship-granting organization, rather than paying for their tuition personally.
Vance singled out nine universities that he said merited further investigation for J-1 visa fraud, saying they used the program in greater proportions than their counterparts.
The universities were Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech; Arizona State; and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or MIT. Stanford said it would cooperate with the investigation. The other universities did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Associated Press writers Heather Hollingsworth in Mission, Kansas and Paul Wiseman and Annie Ma in Washington D.C. contributed. Ortutay reported from Oakland, Calif.

sources.news_title: VP Vance, Sec. of Labor Sonderling Throw a Wrench in the Tech Sector's Abuse of Foreign Employment
sources.text:
As part of the Fraud Task Force crackdown, Vice President JD Vance, Vice Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, and Dept. of Labor OIG Anthony D’Esposito announced huge moves on the H-1B visa program and specifically the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM).
Vance pinpointed the Microsoft Corporation as a chief offender of foreign labor abuse and the actions the task force planned to take.
Vance began:
The H-1B visa is how people get into the country. The PERM program is how they stay in the United States to begin with. Now, there has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, who has abused this system more than Microsoft.
Microsoft laid off, last year, 6,000 American workers. At the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign, indentured servants. Now that is a scandalous system that we've allowed in this country for far too long. But thanks to the work of this task force, and thanks to the empowerment of the President of the United States, we are going to stop it.
Because thanks to an ongoing investigation, we have decided to suspend the PERM program for Microsoft, which means they will no longer be able to apply, no longer be able to take those H-1B visas and apply for permanent resident status within the United States of America.
Now our message to Microsoft and to any other foreign or domestic corporation is quite simple: We obviously want you to thrive in the United States of America. We want people to invest in the United States of America. Particularly the American technology sector, we are the biggest boosters of your industry, we want you to continue to grow and employ a lot of people.
But we want you to employ American workers. And so our message to Microsoft is, you're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants.

Vice President JD Vance announces the suspension of the PERM Program for Microsoft: "Thanks to an ongoing investigation, we have decided to suspend the PERM program for Microsoft, which means they will no longer be able to take those H-1Bs and apply for permanent resident status within the United States of America. Now our message to Microsoft and to any other foreign or domestic corporation is quite simple. We obviously want you to thrive in the United States of America. We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector. We’re the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers. And so our message to Microsoft is, you’re great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants."
— Vice President JD Vance (@VP) October 8, 2026
Vance then gave high praise and credit to the newly minted Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling for doing the research to spearhead this latest initiative to combat the fraud and waste in these employment programs. Vance called Sonderling to the podium for remarks.
Sonderling announced that along with Microsoft, the Department of Labor would also suspend the PERM program for some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini.
Sonderling said:
This administration knows that American workers are the best and the brightest in the world. These jobs that were stolen from them should have gone, and will now go to the Americans first. Not foreigners, and especially not foreign fraudsters.
Thanks to President Trump, Vice President, and the task force, we are cutting off the head of the snake. The companies that have enabled this abuse for decades[...]
And also due to multiple, active federal investigations, the Department of Labor is suspending Microsoft and Adode from the program.
So what does this mean?: We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving this company.
Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers.
WATCH:
We’re cutting off the head of the snake and protecting American Workers. Beginning today, @USDOL is SUSPENDING Microsoft and Adobe among other companies from the permanent visa program. After a pipeline of systemic fraud has flooded our country for years with foreign labor, we’re putting an end to it today. We are taking action under the direction of @POTUS and with the leadership of @VP and @USLaborIG on the @WHFraudTF—DELIVERING for the American People, protecting their money, and punishing fraudsters. 💪 🇺🇸
— Secretary Keith Sonderling (@Sonderling47) October 8, 2026

Combatting fraud and abuse in these visa programs is not only saving money for the American taxpayer, but upholding and protecting the American worker. For decades, Chambers of Commerce and major corporations have turned a blind eye to the manipulation of these programs and dumped foreign workers into the mix at the expense of American ingenuity and sweat equity.

The HISTORIC action we’re taking today is a critical first step to END the MISUSE of the visa process and protect American Workers. The suspensions of these companies from the permanent visa program are a HUGE WIN for hardworking Americans. sources.news_title: JD Vance Forced to Eat His Words Immediately After Trashing Microsoft
sources.text:
JD Vance Forced to Eat His Words Immediately After Trashing Microsoft
The vice president attacked Microsoft on the same day Trump is planning to give a top award to its CEO.
From left: Homeland Security adviser Stephen Miller, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Vice President JD Vance, and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling during an October 8 press conference on the H-1B visa program
Alex WROBLEWSKI/AFP/Getty Images
From left: Homeland Security adviser Stephen Miller, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Vice President JD Vance, and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling during an October 8 press conference on the H-1B visa program
Vice President JD Vance was forced to eat his words in real time, accusing Microsoft of hiring too many foreign workers on the same day President Trump plans to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
Vance criticized Microsoft while announcing the tech company would be temporarily suspended from sponsoring H-1B visa workers seeking green cards.
“We obviously want you to thrive in the United States of America. We want people to invest in the United States of America. Particularly the American technology sector, we’re the bigger boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ … American workers,” Vance said at his Thursday morning news conference. “So our message to Microsoft is, ‘You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.’”
This is a common argument against the H-1B work visa program, which allows foreign professionals to work in the United States.
Microsoft has abused the US visa program, @VP Vance says. "You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers, and if you're a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who, frankly, shouldn't be in the United States of America to begin with," he said.
Vance called for Congress to reform H1B program.
Vance was questioned about the ironic timing of his comment just minutes later, and tried to have it both ways.
“You had some harsh words for Microsoft at the top of your speech just then,” a reporter raised. “In that case, why is President Trump awarding the nation’s top technological medal to the CEO of Microsoft this afternoon?”
“Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them, they do a lot of important things. They also laid off 6,000 American workers while replacing them with 6,300 H-1Bs,” Vance replied. “And our message to Microsoft is not that we wanna harm your company, it’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.”
Q: You had some harsh words for Microsoft at the job of your speech, so why is Trump today awarding the nation's top tech medal to Microsoft's CEO?
JD VANCE: Microsoft is a great American company. They also laid off 6,000 Americans workers while replacing them with 6,300 H-1Bs. https://t.co/39KwDNTe62
The last time Vance waded into the H-1B debate he ended up dragging his wife, Usha Vance, the daughter of Indian immigrants, into the fray.
“You can believe on the one hand that there’s a lot of fraud in the H-1B system, while also believing that there are people who have come to the United States in the past who have enriched this country. And look, I’m married to the daughter of immigrants from India, and, you know, I love my in-laws.… They’ve been great contributors to the United States of America,” he said at a Turning Point USA event last spring. “But I also think when you become an American citizen … one of the obligations of citizens is that you have to think about the best interest of the country, and not the country you came from before.”
Vance seems to have applied that thinking to Microsoft today—perhaps without running it by Trump first.
Trump’s Latest Midterms Tantrum Goes Too Far for Fox News
Donald Trump freaked out over Fox News interviewing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on the set of The Story With Martha MacCallum for Fox News
Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images
Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on the set of The Story With Martha MacCallum for Fox News
The president is making an enemy out of Fox News.
The conservative media behemoth publicly defended its reporting this week, rebuking a wave of Republican backlash that began after host Martha MacCallum interviewed Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in August.
“Someone didn’t necessarily like that,” Fox News Media president Jay Wallace told Axios Thursday, seemingly referring to Donald Trump. “But that’s what we do.”
For years, Fox News blurred the line between legitimate news coverage and conservative entertainment. The network veered toward sycophancy once Trump entered office the first time, offering buddy-buddy interviews to the presidential Cabinet while dampening the reach of critical stories such as the Epstein files. (Fox News mentioned the prolific child sex trafficker hundreds fewer times than its major broadcast competitors.)
But apparently, Republicans got too comfortable with Fox’s bent knee. Once network executives decided to air interviews with Democratic competitors—such as El-Sayed—the floodgates opened.
First, the outcry was private. White House aides put in calls to the network, complaining that Fox’s angle on El-Sayed would only help him in the tight Michigan race.
But the fury bubbled to the public sphere this week, when Trump decided to take the issue to Truth Social.
“FoxNews spends more time covering the Jihadist and Dumocrat candidates than they do the good old fashioned Republicans, the people that have saved America, and are making it great again,” Trump posted on Truth Social Tuesday.
Trump further claimed that MacCallum had offered El-Sayed a “softball interview.”
“She never interviews me like that. They don’t show my record breaking Rallies the morning after, but others do, and that’s what MAGA is watching. Fox is promoting the Dumocrats, not the Republicans and MAGA. They have totally lost their way!” he added.
Republican strategists also chimed in. Jason Roe, a Michigan-based GOP operative, told Axios that the network was doing El-Sayed a “favor.”
“It’s only helping him reach center-right voters,” Roe said. “But they are in business to make money, and he attracts eyeballs.”
In another post Wednesday evening, Trump went full Islamophobe, referring to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” (the candidate’s full first name is Abdulrahman) and deriding him as a “Terrorist Sympathizer.”
El-Sayed responded to the attack Thursday morning, arguing that Trump is “not just attacking me.”
“He’s attacking all of us. He thinks so low of us. He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office. He thinks we don’t know any better,” El-Sayed wrote on X. “It’s time for change.”
“Go After Anybody”: ICE Gets Terrifying Marching Orders in California
ICE has launched a new crackdown just weeks before the midterms.
Pat Greenhouse/The Boston Globe/Getty Images
Immigration and Customs Enforcement has quietly launched a 45-day immigration crackdown in California ahead of the midterm elections, instructing its officers to “go after anybody.”
The so-called “Operation Safe California” has not been formally announced yet, but two sources told the Washington Examiner Wednesday that operations have been underway for several days.
One source told the outlet that officers were “told to go after anybody, they can pick up anybody.”
The Examiner suggested that means that federal agents will target any undocumented immigrants, not just people with criminal records. There is no evidence to suggest that ICE has ever been so discerning.
News of this secret operation comes as early voting began this week in California, which has been a consistenttargetfor punishment by the Trump administration. Voting rights groups cited an ICE detention that took place in Santa Maria, California, on Monday in the same area that voters had to pass through to reach a ballot drop box.
This latest surge of ICE activity comes more than a year after federal agents descended on Los Angeles in June 2025, which led to widespread protests and violent encounters with law enforcement. Of the hundreds of people detained as part of those raids, seven in 10 people had no criminal convictions.
A second source told the Examiner that “management want numbers.” Last year, White House deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructed ICE to arrest 3,000 immigrants a day, a demand that has overwhelmed the agency and resulted in inhumane and degrading detention practices. Now it seems, the Trump administration plans to turn up the temperature.
Trump Official Hides Damning Report on Israel Killing Americans
David Milstein, a senior adviser to U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee in Jerusalem, is suppressing (and editing) reports on Israeli violence.
A Turkish police officer holds a picture of Turkish American activist Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, who was shot dead by Israeli forces while protesting against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, during her funeral on September 14, 2024.
Murat Kocabas/Middle East Images/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images
A Turkish police officer holds a picture of Turkish American activist Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, who was shot dead by Israeli forces while protesting against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, during her funeral on September 14, 2024.
American diplomats are supposed to represent the interests of the U.S. above everything else.
David Milstein, an aide to U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, was running cover for the Israeli government, suppressing reports critical of Israeli actions, The New York Timesreports. Milstein, according to several unnamed sources, quashed reports from the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem documenting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank—including against Americans.
Milstein sent a cable from the embassy to Washington praising Israel for cracking down on Israeli settler violence, when in reality, embassy staff had drafted a report saying that the Israeli government wasn’t taking action. After Congress raised concerns about how Israeli authorities and settlers have killed nine American citizens, Milstein suppressed another embassy report, hindering lawmakers from investigating further.
Milstein also demanded any communications from the embassy’s section on Palestinian affairs go through him. This led to the embassy’s cables dropping from several per week to only a few per month, sources told the Times. They said that this kind of intervention is unprecedented for the embassy, and is preventing the U.S. government from getting accurate information about Israel from diplomatic channels.
Trump has rarely criticized Israel or Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during his second term as president, and he chose to appoint Huckabee, a Christian Zionist and staunch supporter of Israel, as ambassador. It’s not clear if Milstein’s actions have Huckabee’s blessing, but human rights groups and U.S. allies have raised concerns about all of these issues.
Last month, Canada, France, and the U.K. announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. That’s unlikely to happen in the U.S. anytime soon—and in fact the U.S. has threatened tariffs in response to the sanctions—but one would still expect U.S. diplomats to accurately document what is happening where they are stationed. In the case of Israel, however, the truth is actively being hidden.
Trump Does Nothing as Supporter Attacks Protester at a Rally
Donald Trump wandered aimlessly around the stage as the attack happened and cracked a joke.
Christopher Lee/Bloomberg/Getty Images
President Donald Trump did nothing as one of his rallygoers attacked a peaceful protester.
Trump struggled to get through his address at a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, Wednesday night as his remarks were repeatedly interrupted by at least seven separate protesters.
As one demonstrator made his way out of the arena through the jeering crowd, a rallygoer in a red hat seized the protester’s shirt and yanked his hair, pulling him to the floor.
Other rallygoers appeared to intervene—but not the president of the United States. Instead, he basked in the roar of an angry crowd, wandering aimlessly around the stage. “Let me ask you a question, is there anything like a Trump rally? Is there anything like it?” Trump asked, smiling broadly.
Wow Trump gets heckled in Texas and the protester gets assaulted by a member of the crowd. https://t.co/Wm83sXcvgG
In a separate incident, a rallygoer wearing a white cowboy hat stalked after two protesters as they were directed out of the arena. The rallygoer smacked one of the protesters’ baseball hats off and followed them threateningly, pumping his fists. He even appeared to lunge or kick one of the protesters, before being held back by a security officer.
Trump’s unwillingness to condemn his supporters’ violence (and in many cases, his decision to encourage it) is obviously nothing new. But the failure to address violence that unfolds before his own eyes is still shameful behavior from any leader—let alone the president of the United States.
Speaking at the rally, the president told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here,” and claimed they were “paid by enemies of our nation.” After the sixth interruption, Trump tried to laugh it off. “You know, I never talk about looks of a person, but those are really bad looking people,” Trump said.

sources.news_title: US Freezes Green Card Route for Microsoft, Infosys, Tata; Vance Says 'Visa Fraud'
sources.text: New Delhi: The United States government has announced it will no longer allow a number of tech giants including Microsoft and Indian IT majors to sponsor H1-B visa workers seeking green cards, in a massive blow to thousands of skilled Indian workers seeking tech jobs and permanent resident status in the country.The announcement, which impacts workers from around the world and not just India, came during a press conference on visa fraud addressed by US vice president J.D. Vance, labour secretary Keith Sonderling and others including US Attorney General Todd Blanche and Stephen Miller, the White House Deputy Chief of Staff.“Our message to Microsoft is: you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance, who leads the administration’s anti-fraud task force, said at the press conference, Politico reports.Vance referred to layoffs announced by Microsoft, while Sonderling said the decision covered Adobe and a handful of major Indian tech companies with operations and employees or partnerships in the United States.Citing 6,000 layoffs at Microsoft in 2025, Vance said the company added 6,300 H-1B workers and referred to the H1-B programme as “rife with fraud over the last several years, probably the last several decades”.AI-driven job losses, techies in dragnetA Reuters tracker of job losses due to Artificial Intelligence (AI) said job losses at Microsoft would impact over 2% of its workforce, or 4,800 employees since 2025.Multiple well-known Indian tech majors in the IT services sector featured among those being suspended from the US’s Permanent Labour Certification Programme (known as PERM) during the same press conference.“I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini,” Sonderling said.The certificate is the route available to US companies through which they can sponsor foreign workers for green cards. It requires companies to attest that no suitable American candidate is available for the job. The suspension means they will not be able to sponsor green cards.The restrictions are understood to apply until the US investigates the politically sensitive ‘visa fraud’ allegation that is a political hot potato in election season in the US.“This announcement today should send and does send a strong signal to every single employer in the United States that the Trump Administration will not tolerate discrimination against American workers,” Blanche said at the press conference.US President Donald Trump, via an executive order signed on March 16 this year, set up a Task Force to Eliminate Fraud to coordinate a national strategy against “waste, fraud and abuse” in federal benefit programmes.Vance heads this task force and the Federal Trade Commission and the US Department of Justice are part of the initiative, along with scores of enforcement and support teams from government departments.While the programme was understood to focus on frauds across the board, especially welfare fraud, the attention has lately come to settle on alleged immigration fraud, scanning both the H1-B and J-1 visa programmes.The latter programme is applicable to US universities accepting international students and software or software service outsourcing firms.Referring to Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini, Sonderling said, “Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers.”“They’ve received over 2,30,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 1,00,000 permanent labour certifications,” he said.He characterised these visas as “jobs that were taken from American workers”.Foreign workers versus domestic politicsMiller said America under Donald Trump was the “only country in the world” that had managed to turn an immigration system from being “against its people to for its people”Layoffs by American companies, going by the Reuters tracker of AI-linked job losses, which includes intimations of future sackings by major companies since October 2025, found the highest cuts were in the banking and financial sector and in online marketplaces such as at Amazon, which also is reported to lay off 16,000 employees, as per information until January this year.HSBC Holdings was expected to reduce its workforce by 10% or about 20,000 workers, the tracker said, and Standard Chartered by over 7,000.It is unclear if these are layoffs related to their global business networks and or limited to job cuts for staff located in America.Layoffs are politically sensitive in the United States, especially as they are increasingly linked with the growing ability of Artificial Intelligence to automate tasks performed by humans, which American companies have been quick to both develop and adopt.News of job cuts has of late sparked emotional stories about American workers being disempowered, such as of the laid-off techie in Colorado who drives a school bus after failing to find other work, and the blame often falls on outsourced foreign employees.“H-1B is how they get in, and PERM program is how they stay,” Vance said at Thursday’s event.For the Trump administration, H1-B visas have come to represent workers who, though they may be skilled, find jobs in the US due to seeking lower pay and few perks instead of American workers. As Vance said at Thursday’s press conference, “For every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants.”On J-1 visas, the US Labour Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito specifically stated at the press conference that the administration was specifically targeting nine top universities including Harvard, Stanford and MIT for allegedly using international PhD candidates and scholars to undercut domestic wages.

sources.news_title: Microsoft Is Suspended From Green Card Program. Vance Accuses Company Of H-1B Abuse.
sources.text:
Microsoft Is Suspended From Green Card Program. Vance Accuses Company Of H-1B Abuse.
Microsoft is being suspended from a federal program used by employers seeking green cards for foreign workers, with Vice President JD Vance accusing the company of abusing employment-based immigration rules and displacing American workers.
The action was announced Thursday at a White House news conference, according to AP, which reported that the Trump administration accused Microsoft of fraud in its use of the process.
The suspension concerns permanent labor certification, commonly known as PERM, rather than Microsoft's ability to employ workers through the H-1B visa program generally.
Under the Department of Labor process, companies seeking permanent residency for foreign workers usually must first obtain a labor certification showing that there are not enough qualified U.S. workers available for the job and that hiring the foreign worker will not hurt the wages or working conditions of comparable American employees.
H-1B visas, by contrast, allow companies to temporarily employ foreign workers in specialty occupations. Some H-1B workers later pursue permanent residency through employer-sponsored green card applications that require PERM certification.
Vance said Thursday that Microsoft had laid off American employees while continuing to employ foreign workers.
"If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants," Vance said.
The administration has not publicly detailed the evidence behind that calculation.
Vance said the government's message to large U.S. companies was that they should prioritize hiring American workers.
Microsoft did not immediately respond to AP's request for comment.
The action comes as the administration steps up enforcement across several programs that allow foreign students and workers to live or work in the United States.
In September, President Donald Trump extended restrictions on certain H-1B workers for another year, saying the program had been used by some employers to replace U.S. workers with lower-paid foreign labor.
The White House extended a requirement that certain H-1B petitions for workers outside the United States be accompanied by a $100,000 payment, subject to national-interest exceptions.
A separate White House order directed federal agencies to increase coordination and enforcement around the H-1B system.
The administration said government investigations had identified cases involving displacement of U.S. workers, misrepresentation of job requirements and questionable foreign qualifications. Those findings formed part of the administration's justification for tightening oversight of the program. The Microsoft action involves a different part of the immigration system.
PERM is administered by the Labor Department's Office of Foreign Labor Certification and is generally the first major step for employers seeking employment-based permanent residency for foreign workers.
The Labor Department requires employers to test the U.S. labor market before receiving certification, including conducting recruitment and showing that qualified American workers were not available for the position.
Government enforcement against companies using PERM is not unprecedented. In May, the Department of Labor suspended processing of permanent labor certification applications from data software company Cloudera for 180 days after the Justice Department alleged the company had used a recruitment process that prevented qualified U.S. workers from applying for technology positions.
The administration is also tightening rules affecting international students seeking U.S. work experience.
A Department of Homeland Security proposal published this week would require universities to pay $70,000 when first recommending an international student for Optional Practical Training, or OPT, and $30,000 for subsequent periods of training.
OPT allows students with F-1 visas to temporarily work in jobs connected to their field of study. The proposed fees are not yet in effect and remain subject to the federal rulemaking process. Vance also said that nine universities warranted further investigation over their use of J-1 exchange visas.
Microsoft is one of the biggest U.S. technology companies and has long relied on highly skilled workers in areas including software engineering, cloud computing and artificial intelligence.
The Labor Department processed more than 112,000 PERM applications during the first three quarters of fiscal 2026, including more than 104,000 certifications, according to Department of Labor data. Software developers alone accounted for more than 23,000 of the certifications, or about 23% of the total.
Microsoft shares were little changed Thursday after the announcement. The stock was trading around $529.70, after closing Wednesday at $529.76, and has gained roughly 7.5% over the past month.
