sources.news_title: Trump Admin Cracks Down On Foreign Worker Fraud: Bans MSFT From H1-B Program, Probes 9 Colleges Over J-1 Visas, Hikes Costs For Students
sources.text:
Trump Admin Cracks Down On Foreign Worker Fraud: Bans MSFT From H1-B Program, Probes 9 Colleges Over J-1 Visas, Hikes Costs For Students
In the last 24 hours, the Trump administration has announced three major efforts to crack down on foreign worker/student visa fraud.
First, US Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday that the federal government is suspending tech giant Microsoft from a program to apply for green cards for workers who come to the U.S. to live and work using an H-1B visa as it accuses the company of fraud.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” said Vice President JD Vance in a White House news conference announcing the decision.
Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling added that some of the largest IT firms in the world would also be suspended from that program, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCO and Capgemini, as well as Adobe.
Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Second, the Trump administration is going after nine elite universities on suspicion of visa fraud, accusing them of unlawfully benefiting financially from hiring and admitting foreign nationals.
Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, and MIT are under examination by federal investigators, Vice President JD Vance announced Thursday, suggesting the schools are exploiting the J-1 visa program to import cheaper students from overseas and skirt employment obligations to US citizens.
“Something weird is going on at these universities,” said Vance.
“They’re using these visas way too much. They’re using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop.”
The Labor Department is establishing a visa fraud strike team as part of the probe and subpoenas have already been sent to the schools.
“Nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” said Labor Department watchdog Anthony D’Esposito, who reported that 61% of post-grad students at US universities come from overseas.
“American taxpayers send billions of dollars to these universities to support research and innovation. They deserve to know where that money is be, where is going, and whether it’s being used lawfully.”
And finally, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is considering a new rule that would impose major fees for foreign students seeking to work in the United States.
The proposed rule, announced by the Trump administration on Oct. 7, would require colleges and universities to pay a $70,000 fee for each nonimmigrant student applying to participate in the Optional Practical Training program.
The program authorizes foreign students to temporarily work in the United States in jobs related to their field of study either during or after their time in school.
As Timothy Frudd reports further for The Epoch Times, the new proposal comes after the Trump administration was blocked last month from implementing limitations on F-1 visas, which allow nonimmigrant students to live and study in the United States.
DHS said Wednesday that the proposed rule is intended to reduce the influx of cheap labor into the United States, curb fraud and abuse, protect American workers, and strengthen the integrity of the immigration system.
"Optional Practical Training was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement.
"DHS is upskilling OPT to require foreign students to justify their worth to employers. American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor."
In addition to the initial $70,000 fee for each nonimmigrant student participating in the optional practical training program, colleges and universities would also be required to pay a $30,000 fee for each renewal or extension of the program's authorization for students.
Under the program, F-1 nonimmigrant students are required to receive a recommendation from a designated school official before applying for employment authorization with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.
Students participating in the program are typically eligible to work in the United States for one year after graduation.
However, some students with degrees in science, technology, engineering, or mathematics are eligible to work for an additional two years.
More than 294,000 foreign students participated in the optional practical training program during the 2024-2025 academic year, according to the President's Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration.
In Wednesday's announcement, DHS said it was proposing the new rule in response to fraud and abuse discovered by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program.
As the program has expanded, schools, officials, employers, and F-1 nonimmigrant students have attempted to exploit regulations, including "problematic worksites and 'pay-to-stay' visa schemes," according to DHS.
The department suggested the fees would encourage colleges and universities to employ additional oversight and be more selective of students recommended for the training program.
In response, Fanta Aw, CEO of nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said in a statement that the program provides foreign students with the opportunity to have hands-on experience.
She said international students involved in the program also fill labor shortages in science, technology, engineering, or mathematics fields.
"Imposing this new fee structure on Optional Practical Training is the latest in a series of developments that creates deep uncertainty for international students," Aw said.
"Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership."
A federal judge blocked another Trump administration rule on Sept. 14 that would limit students on F-1 visas to four years in the United States before requiring them to seek approval from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to stay longer.
DHS said the limitation on F-1 visas was needed to address national security risks, including foreign spying at universities in the United States.
Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, who blocked the Trump administration from implementing the law while a legal challenge moved forward in court, said DHS did not explain how the rule would deter future spying or acts of sabotage.
In May 2025, the Trump administration attempted to revoke Harvard University's certification to enroll foreign students under the Student and Exchange Visitor Program.
Harvard responded by suing the administration, and a federal judge blocked the government from preventing the university from enrolling foreign students through the program.

sources.news_title: Microsoft, Adobe blocked from green-card program amid visa fraud crackdown
sources.text:
Microsoft, Adobe blocked from green-card program amid visa fraud crackdown
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Vice President JD Vance announced Thursday that the Trump administration is suspending Microsoft, Adobe and six major outsourcing firms from a program used to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency as it cracks down on alleged abuse of H-1B and J-1 visas.
The administration also opened investigations into nine universities, alleging employers and schools have used the programs to undercut American workers.
Microsoft, Adobe and outsourcing firms blocked from PERM program
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini will no longer be able to submit new or have pending applications processed through the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM. The process is generally an employer’s first step in sponsoring a foreign worker for an employment-based green card.
Vance said the PERM suspensions will remain in place "as long as it needs to," adding that the administration has tools to extend them indefinitely but wants companies to change their hiring practices.
When asked what made the conduct fraudulent, Vance said employers must certify that a foreign worker has specialized skills that cannot be filled by an American worker. The administration alleges those certifications are false when companies use the program to replace U.S. workers with lower-paid foreign employees.
Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers,” Sonderling said, claiming they received more than 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and more than 100,000 permanent labor certifications.
Vance singled out Microsoft, saying the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
“Microsoft, you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
The suspension comes as Trump is scheduled to honor Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella later Thursday with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a White House science summit. The action applies to Microsoft’s use of the PERM program, not Nadella personally.
Vance argued that the H-1B program — intended for employers that cannot fill specialized jobs with U.S. workers — has become “rife with fraud.” He alleged some companies post ineffective job advertisements, then cite a lack of applicants to justify hiring foreign workers who are paid less and can lose their ability to remain in the United States if they lose their jobs.
He also targeted foreign outsourcing firms that help employers recruit H-1B workers, claiming visa holders earn about $20,000 less than similarly positioned American workers. Vance said workers recruited through outsourcing firms earn about $48,000 less than comparable Americans.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department is actively investigating companies that favor foreign workers over Americans.
He explained potential consequences could include criminal prosecutions, civil lawsuits to recover money and action against companies or individual leaders, depending on the results of the investigations.
Nine universities face J-1 visa fraud investigations
Additionally, the administration said it has served subpoenas and opened investigations into alleged J-1 visa abuse at Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State and MIT.
Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito said investigators will examine whether the universities improperly used J-1 classifications to avoid employment obligations, exploit taxpayer-funded programs or undermine American workers. He said the inquiry will also scrutinize possible foreign influence and financial relationships involving federally funded research.
Nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” D’Esposito said.
Vance said the schools use J-1 visa holders for federally funded grants at a rate of about 61%, compared with a 38% national average. He alleged the schools are using the program to undercut the wages of American graduate students and researchers, who he said earn about $20,000 more in comparable positions.
Administration expands crackdown on foreign-worker visa programs
D’Esposito announced the creation of a visa fraud strike team and said Labor Department inspector general investigations since Vance’s fraud task force was created have contributed to 171 indictments, 203 convictions, 80 arrests and more than $1 billion identified for taxpayers.
Vance urged Congress to overhaul the H-1B system but said the administration would use its existing authority in the meantime.
“Never believe the lie that Americans are not good enough to build a future for Americans,” he said.
The announcement follows the Labor Department inspector general’s nationwide investigation into alleged fraud and human trafficking involving H-1B and PERM programs.
It also comes as the Department of Homeland Security proposes a $70,000 fee for schools sponsoring international students for Optional Practical Training, or OPT. DHS said the proposal is meant to combat fraud and protect U.S. workers; public comments are due within 30 days.

sources.news_title: Why the US Cut Microsoft, Adobe From Green Card Sponsorship
sources.text:
For years, the deal for a foreign software engineer in the U.S. has been simple. Come in on a temporary H-1B visa, do good work, and your employer sponsors you for a green card. The visa gets you in the door. The green card is why you stay.
That deal just broke for people working at some of the biggest companies in tech. The US Labor Department says it won't accept new applications from nine companies or process the ones already in the queue.
On October 8, 2026, Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCLTech and Capgemini were suspended from PERM, the labour certification process employers use to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency.
Why did the US suspend companies from the PERM program?
The official reason is said to be because of 'fraud'. Officials say these companies have been using the program to swap American workers for cheaper foreign hires and push down wages, though they haven't made public the evidence behind those claims.
The crackdown has been building for months. In July, the Labor Department's Inspector General opened an investigation into alleged abuse of the H-1B and PERM programs, looking at things like fake recruitment, wage kickbacks and keeping visa workers unpaid between projects. In September, Cognizant and Cloudera had their PERM filings frozen, and public data showed Adobe's pending cases sitting on hold weeks before the company was named. What started as an investigation has now become a policy lever.

Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those…

The United States has suspended eight major technology companies, including Microsoft, Adobe, Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant and Capgemini, from a key programme allowing employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency.
The decision, announced on October 8 by US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling alongside Vice President JD Vance, is part of the Trump administration’s crackdown on alleged abuses of employment-based immigration programmes.
Under the suspension, the US Department of Labor will stop accepting new applications and processing pending applications involving the eight companies under the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme.

The administration accused major technology companies of relying heavily on foreign workers while laying off American employees.
Vance singled out Microsoft, questioning why the company continued sponsoring foreign employees while cutting jobs in the United States.
According to the administration, the eight companies have collectively sought nearly three million foreign workers since 2009, receiving more than 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications.
Microsoft defended its employment practices, saying approximately 80% of its H-1B applications in the previous fiscal year involved extensions or changes of status for existing employees rather than new hires.
The suspension does not automatically cancel existing H-1B visas or prevent affected companies from continuing to employ foreign workers. However, it restricts an important pathway for employees seeking permanent residency in the United States.
The move is part of President Donald Trump’s broader immigration policy, which seeks to tighten employment-based immigration rules and prioritise American workers.
The decision could have significant implications for foreign technology professionals seeking long-term employment and permanent residency in the United States. (Newswire)

sources.news_title: US freezes Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys green-card applications
sources.text:
The Trump administration has frozen some green-card filings by Microsoft, Adobe and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine top universities, widening a visa crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.
The twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs - potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers - while putting some of the country's top research universities on notice.
"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft," Vice President JD Vance said.
He said the company laid off 6000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3000 green cards.
The announcement about the permanent labor certification process — PERM — came hours before Trump was due to give Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
Under PERM, required for most employment-based green cards, employers must show that hiring a foreign worker will not harm US workers' wages or job opportunities.
Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, according to data from the US labor department.
The company said in a statement that about 80 percent of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers.
In July, the company said it would cut 4800 jobs, or about 2.1 percent of its global workforce.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.
"We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said.
He said these companies had since 2009 sought almost three million foreign workers, and had received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications.
Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to US immigration data.
Vance said the suspensions would last "as long as it needs to," adding that the administration wants the companies to change how they hire.
He said some companies post ineffective job ads, then cite a lack of applicants to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers.
Microsoft said in its statement that it pays its H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.
“The immediate financial impact on major technology companies may be relatively limited at this moment, but the longer-term implications for innovation and competitiveness could be much more significant," said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management.
Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment.
Nasscom, India's IT industry body, said Indian tech companies in the US had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, and relatively few of their workers sought green cards through the PERM process.
Crackdown widens
The suspensions are the latest in a series of steps against skilled-worker programs.
In September last year, the US Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called "Project Firewall" as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time US$100,000 fee ($143,700) on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad.
During President Donald Trump's second term, companies have faced growing pressure to keep jobs and production in the United States rather than move them overseas.
The action comes despite closer ties between the administration and tech leaders, who are lobbying for lighter AI regulation.
Universities under scrutiny
Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages.
The nine schools also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.
D'Esposito said investigators would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa abuse were compromising federally funded research.
“It could have an enormous economic impact on the whole US economy,” said Sarah Spreitzer, a vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents. International students historically spent US$40 billion a year while in the US, she said.
The probe deepens the administration's long-running fight with Harvard over foreign students. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed the university over alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with immigration law.
Harvard called that subpoena "unfounded retribution" but said it would comply as far as the law requires.

sources.news_title: US suspends Microsoft from Green Card sponsorship programme; company responds: Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who…
sources.text:
The US government has suspended Microsoft from the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM), the process most employers must clear before sponsoring a foreign worker for a Green Card. Vice President JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the move at a press conference in Washington on October 8, and the Labor Department will now neither accept new PERM applications from Microsoft nor process the ones already pending.Vance singled out the company as the worst offender. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” he said, claiming Microsoft laid off around 6,000 American workers last year while employing 6,300 people on H-1B visas and securing nearly 3,000 Green Cards. Microsoft has pushed back, saying the vast majority of its US employees are Americans.
A Vance-led fraud probe is behind Microsoft’s PERM suspension
The suspension follows an investigation by an anti-fraud task force that Vance chairs. Officials argued that PERM is meant for roles needing “hyper-specialized” skills that are hard to find in the US, and accused Microsoft of misrepresenting its needs to replace American staff with cheaper foreign hires.“The H-1B visa is how the people get into the United States in the first place, and then a PERM program is how those employees stay,” Vance said. He also claimed that for every worker Microsoft laid off, it brought in “one and a half foreign indentured servants.” Sonderling said Microsoft was suspended “due to multiple active federal investigations.”Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, according to Labor Department data, so the freeze puts a sizeable pipeline of employee Green Card cases on hold.
Microsoft says most of its H-1B filings were for existing employees
Microsoft responded with a blog post on Thursday. It said about 80% of the roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees, not to hire new people. The rest were for people already living legally in the US, and they make up only 1% of its US workforce.“Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company said. It added that its H-1B wages are among the highest of all filings, and that these employees are paid the same as anyone else doing comparable work.Data from Levels.fyi places Microsoft fourth among H-1B sponsors this year, with 21,706 petitions at a median base salary of $180,710. The company also said in July it would cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1% of its global workforce.
Vance says the Microsoft suspension will last “as long as it needs to”
Vance did not spell out what Microsoft must do to regain access to the programme. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company, it’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans,” he said.The timing stood out. Hours later, President Donald Trump was due to present Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, the country’s highest honour for tech achievement. Just over a week earlier, India-born Nadella, who joined Microsoft in 1992, sat two seats from Vance at a White House luncheon on AI.The move extends a wider crackdown on skilled-worker visas ahead of the November midterms, which last September brought a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions. For Microsoft employees already in the queue, the wait was long to begin with: PERM applications took an average of 336 days to process in August. Now it has no end date at all.

sources.news_title: US Warns Microsoft Against Replacing American Workers With Foreign Labour
sources.text:
United States Vice President JD Vance has issued a direct warning to Microsoft, saying the technology giant must not lay off American workers and replace them with foreign labour under the country’s H-1B visa programme.
Vance said the administration wants American technology companies to expand and attract investment but insisted that such growth must translate into more jobs for US workers.
His remarks come amid an intensifying crackdown by the Donald Trump administration on alleged abuses of the H-1B visa system, which allows US employers to temporarily hire foreign workers for specialised occupations.
“We obviously want you to thrive in the United States of America. We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector. We are the biggest boosters of your industry,” Vance said.
“We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers. And so our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
Vance also accused major US corporations, particularly technology companies, of exploiting the H-1B programme by using foreign workers as a cheaper alternative to American employees.
He argued that the visa programme was originally intended to enable companies to recruit highly specialised foreign talent where qualified American workers were unavailable.
“The H-1B visa program is meant to allow companies to bring in really the best of the best from outside the United States of America for positions that are completely impossible to fill with American workers,” he said.
However, Vance alleged that the system has become vulnerable to widespread abuse.
“Unfortunately, the program has become rife with fraud over the last several years, probably the last several decades,” he said.
According to the vice president, some companies allegedly advertise vacancies in ways that make it difficult to attract American applicants before claiming they cannot find suitable domestic workers.
“And here’s the basic game that American corporations and foreign corporations will play,” Vance said.
“They will say, maybe they’ll put an advertisement in a small town newspaper. They’ll go out there and say that we have advertised for a position with our company and nobody is responding to it.”
He alleged that companies then use the lack of applicants as justification for bringing in foreign workers and displacing American employees.
“And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured service,” he added

sources.news_title: US Suspends Infosys, TCS, Wipro and Cognizant From PERM Programme Over Alleged Fraud
sources.text:
The US Department of Labour on October 8 suspended Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies, Cognizant and Capgemini from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, a key step in the employment-based green-card process for foreign workers.
Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department would not accept new or process pending PERM applications involving the companies, while Vice President JD Vance accused firms of misusing worker-visa programmes and urged them to prioritise American workers. The administration said the action was driven by alleged abuse and, in Microsoft’s and Adobe’s cases, multiple active federal investigations.
‘Hundreds Of Thousands Of Jobs’
Sonderling said the affected companies had collectively requested almost three million foreign workers since 2009, received more than 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and secured over 100,000 permanent labour certifications. He claimed this represented “hundreds of thousands of jobs” taken from American workers.
Vance singled out Microsoft, alleging that it laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025 while receiving more than 6,000 H-1B approvals and filing 3,682 PERM applications, with nearly 1,000 linked to positions from which American workers had been laid off. “Stop defrauding the American worker,” Vance said, urging companies to stop using foreign workers for jobs that Americans could perform.
PERM Suspension
PERM, or Permanent Labour Certification, generally requires an employer to demonstrate that there are no qualified, willing and available American workers for a particular position before sponsoring a foreign worker for permanent residency.
The latest suspension therefore creates uncertainty for employees whose green-card applications depend on their employers completing this stage. However, the move does not itself cancel existing H-1B visas or already-approved green cards. The Trump administration’s action comes amid a broader crackdown on employment-based immigration, including heightened scrutiny of H-1B visas and a separate investigation into J-1 visa practices at nine universities.
The Logical Indian’s Perspective
Protecting local employment and ensuring that immigration programmes are not misused are legitimate policy goals, but allegations of fraud or unfair hiring practices should be established through transparent investigations and due process rather than assumed from the outset.
At the same time, foreign professionals working legally in the America should not be treated as disposable numbers in a political debate: behind every delayed green-card application is a person whose career, family and future may be affected. A fair system should protect American workers while also respecting the contribution and rights of skilled migrants.

sources.news_title: US Labor Department Suspends Microsoft Adobe And Six Other Firms
sources.text:
US Labor Department suspends Microsoft Adobe and six other firms
The U.S. Labor Department suspended Microsoft, Adobe, and six other tech firms from a green card program on October 8, 2026. The U.S. Labor Department announced the decision on Thursday, October 8, 2026, immediately halting the companies’ ability to sponsor foreign employees for permanent residency.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, speaking at a White House press conference, confirmed the suspensions from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program. He was joined by Vice President JD Vance and Attorney General Todd Blanche. The move targets what officials described as widespread fraud and abuse of visa programs that they claim disadvantages American workers.
Labor Department suspensions target tech and IT giants
The U.S. Department of Labor’s action effectively freezes the path to a green card for thousands of foreign workers employed by the affected companies. The suspension means the department will not accept or process any new applications for permanent labor certification from the firms, which is a mandatory first step for sponsoring most employment-based green cards.
Alongside tech behemoths Microsoft and Adobe, the suspension list includes major global IT and outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini. While the move doesn’t revoke existing H-1B temporary work visas, it creates immense uncertainty for employees who saw the PERM process as their route to remaining in the U.S. permanently.
This move has been a point of contention within the tech industry, a sector that has faced various government warnings, including a recent one from the Consumer Technology Association on other policy matters.
According to Secretary Sonderling, the scale of foreign worker recruitment by these companies has been enormous. “Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers,” Sonderling stated. “They’ve received over 230,000 H-1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications.
That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers.” The action signals a significant shift in enforcement and a direct challenge to the hiring models of some of the world’s largest tech corporations.
Full list of suspended companies
The Department of Labor has suspended the following eight companies from the Permanent Labor Certification program:
- Microsoft
- Adobe
- Cognizant
- Infosys
- Tata
- Wipro
- HCL
- Capgemini
Administration alleges widespread fraud and abuse
Officials justified the unprecedented suspensions by citing “multiple active federal investigations” and alleging systemic abuse of the visa system. Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft, accusing it of being the company that has “most abused the system.” Vance pointed to Microsoft’s 6,000 layoffs in 2025, claiming the company simultaneously acquired 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
“So we’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first,” Vance declared. He calculated that for every American worker Microsoft laid off, they replaced them with 1.5 “foreign indentured servants.”
The alleged fraud involves a specific tactic where companies purportedly place job advertisements in obscure small-town newspapers. After receiving no responses, they then claim no qualified American workers were available, creating a justification to hire a foreign worker. This approach to talent acquisition stands in contrast to domestic strategies, such as how some firms like Citigroup shortens analyst programs to retain talent in competitive fields.
Microsoft defends hiring practices amid criticism
Microsoft quickly responded to the sharp accusations from the White House, defending its hiring record in a statement. The company asserted that “the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans” and sought to reframe the administration’s narrative about replacing domestic workers.
The Redmond-based software giant provided its own data to counter the government’s claims. “Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees,” the company stated.
This suggests that a large portion of its visa applications are for retaining current staff rather than hiring new foreign replacements for laid-off American workers. Adobe had not issued a public comment at the time of the announcement.
The crackdown comes at an awkward time, as it was announced at the same White House event where President Donald Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Science to several prominent immigrant tech leaders. This included Microsoft’s own CEO, Satya Nadella, who immigrated from India in 1988. This juxtaposition highlights the complex and often contradictory nature of the U.S. debate on high-skilled immigration.
Broader crackdown extends to universities and markets
The administration’s enforcement action is not limited to the eight named corporations. Officials also announced a wider probe into the J-1 visa program, which is used for work-and-study-based exchange programs. Subpoenas have been served to nine of America’s most prestigious universities, including Harvard, Yale, Stanford, MIT, Caltech, Brown, UC Davis, the University of Pittsburgh, and Arizona State University.
Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed the Department of Justice is also pursuing investigations into companies that allegedly favor foreign workers over qualified Americans. The breadth of these actions, from corporate green card programs to academic visas, signals a coordinated, government-wide effort to reshape U.S. immigration and labor policies.
Such direct government interventions can have far-reaching consequences, similar to the market impact seen when the US government moves bitcoin in large quantities.
Wall Street’s reaction to the news was mixed. Shares of Microsoft and Adobe remained relatively stable, trading slightly higher. However, the IT outsourcing firms, which rely heavily on foreign workers, saw their stocks fall. Infosys shares dropped 2.2% and Wipro fell 3.5%, while Cognizant lost about 0.7%.
This divergence indicates that investors are, for now, betting the U.S.-based tech giants are better insulated from the policy’s impact than the global IT service firms.
A complex political landscape
The politics of the announcement were as complex as its policy implications. While castigating some companies for their use of visa programs, Vice President Vance drew a distinction for elite immigrant entrepreneurs. Other leaders being honored at the White House summit included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su, both born in Taiwan, and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk, a native of South Africa.
“It’s one thing if you want to bring in a person like Elon Musk,” Vance commented. “I think 99% of American citizens look at somebody like Elon Musk or Lisa Su…
and they say, obviously, if that person wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America, we support that.” The statement attempts to separate celebrated founders from the rank-and-file skilled workers who form the backbone of many tech operations.
What happens next remains uncertain, but the suspensions have undeniably thrown a wrench into the long-term plans of both the targeted companies and their thousands of foreign national employees.

sources.news_title: US Suspends Infosys TCS Wipro And 5 Others From Green Card Program
sources.text:
In a significant move that could reshape the landscape of the technology industry and immigration, the United States government has announced the suspension of eight major tech corporations from the Program Electronic Review Management (PERM). This decision, which targets some of the most prominent names in the global IT sector, includes Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft, and Adobe. The suspension effectively halts these companies' ability to initiate the green card process for their foreign employees, a move that's expected to have far-reaching consequences for thousands of workers, particularly those holding H-1B visas.
Official Announcement and Key Figures
The announcement was made on Thursday by the United States Labor Secretary, Keith Sonderling. The gravity of the decision was underscored by the presence of high-ranking officials during the briefing, including the head of the US Anti-Fraud Task Force and Vice President JD Vance, while this collective presence signals a coordinated effort by the US administration to tighten oversight on labor certifications and immigration processes related to employment.
According to reports from PTI News, Secretary Sonderling was explicit in his statement regarding the suspension. " He further clarified that the Department of Labor is extending this suspension to include tech giants Microsoft and Adobe as well. This broad sweep covers both traditional outsourcing firms and major software developers, indicating a comprehensive review of how these entities use foreign labor.
Impact on Foreign Workers and Historical Data
The immediate fallout of this decision is the rejection of all new and pending permanent labor certification applications from these eight companies. This creates a significant hurdle for foreign professionals who were in the process of seeking permanent residency in the United States. Secretary Sonderling provided historical context to the scale of these companies' operations, claiming that since 2009, these eight firms have requested approximately 3000000 foreign workers. During this period, they successfully secured approvals for more than 230000 H-1B visas and obtained over 100000 permanent labor certifications.
The US Labor Secretary alleged that these high volumes of foreign hires have directly impacted the employment opportunities available to American citizens. He characterized the situation as a loss of millions of jobs that could have otherwise been filled by US workers. This perspective forms the core of the administration's justification for the suspension, focusing on the protection of the domestic labor market.
Understanding the PERM Program
The Permanent Labor Certification Program, commonly known as PERM, is a critical process managed by the Department of Labor. It allows US employers to hire foreign workers for permanent positions, while however, the program is built on strict prerequisites. Employers must generally demonstrate that there aren't enough qualified, willing, and available US workers to fill the position. Also, they must prove that hiring a foreign worker won't adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.
Once the Department of Labor approves the labor certification, the employer can proceed with an immigrant petition to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), typically through Form I-140. For H-1B visa holders, the PERM process is often the most vital step toward obtaining an employment-based green card. By suspending a company's access to this program, the US government makes it nearly impossible for that employer to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residence, thereby stalling their path to citizenship.
Objectives and Identified Vulnerabilities
The primary objective of the PERM program is to ensure that American workers aren't disadvantaged when employers seek to fill permanent roles with foreign talent, while before a green card sponsorship can occur, the labor-market test must be conducted to verify the lack of available US talent. Concerns arise among US officials when employers are suspected of manipulating or bypassing this test. Fraudulent recruitment practices can create a false impression that no qualified American workers are available, when in reality, they may have been discouraged from applying or excluded from consideration.
The Department of Labor's Inspector General has previously identified several vulnerabilities within the PERM system, while these include the submission of fraudulent applications, the provision of inadequate supporting documentation, and weaknesses in the enforcement of rules after a certification has been granted. The current suspension appears to be a direct response to these systemic concerns, aiming to restore integrity to the labor certification process.

Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the action, while Vice President JD Vance accused companies of using visa programmes to replace Americans and reduce wages.
New Delhi: The United States on Thursday suspended several major technology firms from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme, which allows employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent employment and residency.
US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the decision alongside Vice President JD Vance and the head of the US Anti-Fraud Task Force. He accused the companies of taking jobs away from Americans.

Applications face processing freeze
Sonderling said the government would neither accept new permanent labour certification applications nor process pending applications involving the suspended firms.
“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They’ve received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications,” Sonderling added.
He alleged that their hiring practices had cost American workers hundreds of thousands of jobs.
The certification programme forms part of the employer-sponsored green card process. The announced action concerns permanent labour certification applications.
Vance targets Microsoft hiring
Vance singled out Microsoft and accused it of abusing the system.
“Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025 after certifying that it could not find qualified American employees – yet the company was approved for more than 6,000 H-1Bs and filed 3,682 PERM applications, including nearly 1,000 applications for the same positions as the laid-off American workers,” the vice president said.
He described workers hired through H-1B visas as “foreign indentured servants” and companies that used the programme as “visa mills”.
Vance also alleged that firms used limited job advertisements to claim they could not find suitable American applicants before seeking permission to hire foreign workers.
University visas draw criticism
The vice president also questioned universities’ use of the J-1 visa programme for research scholars.
“Something weird is going on at these universities. They’re using these visas way too much. They’re using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers,” Vance said.
He argued that visa programmes should help companies access skilled talent without reducing American workers’ wages.

Vance Suspends Microsoft's PERM Filings After a Probe Tied 6,000 Layoffs to 6,300 H-1B Hires
The indefinite administrative suspension also applies to Adobe and major IT outsourcers, while officials allege companies made false representations under the PERM process.
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Thursday barred Microsoft from filing new or pending applications to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency, and Vice President JD Vance said the company had abused the program more than any other in the country.
The suspension covers the Labor Department's PERM process, the step that lets an employer seek a green card for a worker already in the United States, often on an H-1B visa. Microsoft did not immediately comment.
Vance, who chairs an anti-fraud task force, said the probe found Microsoft laid off roughly 6,000 American workers last year while employing 6,300 non-citizens it had brought in on H-1B visas. "The H-1B visa is how the people get into the United States in the first place, and then a PERM program is how those employees stay," he said. "There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft."
He described the alleged violation as a false representation, not a paperwork error. "The fraud is that they're making representations when applying for this program that are fundamentally illegitimate and therefore ultimately illegal," he said. At a press conference he added, "Our message to Microsoft is, you're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants." He said the arithmetic was one and a half foreign hires for each layoff. "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one-and-a-half foreign indentured servants."
Sonderling said that since 2009, Microsoft and Adobe together had received about 230,000 H-1B approvals and about 100,000 permanent labor certifications. Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications in Labor Department disclosure data compiled by Permtrack. The suspensions do not, on the statements issued Thursday, revoke visas already issued. They stop the green-card step.
The move sits on a wider crackdown. In September 2025 the department opened "Project Firewall," which has opened about 200 cases and levied millions of dollars in penalties, after a White House proclamation put a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad. Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated over the use of exchange-visitor visas. The administration has at the same time courted the same technology executives whose companies are now named.
PERM requires an employer to attest that it tried to hire a qualified U.S. worker and could not. The department's case is that those attestations were not real when the same firm was cutting thousands of domestic jobs. That is an allegation. No criminal charge was announced Thursday. The bar is administrative and indefinite. A company that wants the certifications processed again will have to deal with a department that has already said it will not take the filings.

The affected companies include Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Cognizant.
The decision, announced by US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling, also impacts Microsoft, Capgemini and Adobe.
“I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini,” Sonderling said, flanked by the head of US Anti-Fraud Task Force and Vice-President JD Vance.
Sonderling said the US government won’t accept “any new or process” any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies.
“Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers. They’ve received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications,” Sonderling informed, accusing these companies of taking away hundreds of thousands of jobs from American workers.
Vance slammed Microsoft, describing it as a company that abused the system the most.
“Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025 after certifying that it could not find qualified American employees… yet the company was approved for more than 6,000 H-1Bs and filed 3,682 PERM applications, including nearly 1,000 applications for the same positions as the laid-off American workers,” the Vice-President said.
The US decision is likely to create uncertainty for Indian IT professionals around future employer-sponsored Green Card applications.
However, suspension of new PERM filings does not automatically cancel existing approved Green Card cases, according to officials.

sources.news_title: Vance suspends Microsoft from green card program over H-1B fraud claims
sources.text:
"For every worker Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants," Vance said Thursday. The White House used that math to suspend Microsoft's green-card sponsorship, without releasing evidence.
Vice President JD Vance announced Thursday that Microsoft is being suspended from the federal program that lets it sponsor green cards for its H-1B visa holders, accusing the company of fraud. The move targets PERM, the Labor Department's permanent labor certification process, not Microsoft's broader ability to hire or retain H-1B workers. "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants," Vance said at a White House briefing, according to the Associated Press.
That line is vivid. The evidence behind it is thin. The administration has not released the specific conduct it considers fraudulent, nor named which filings triggered the suspension. Vance's announcement came packaged with a broader swipe at universities over their use of J-1 student visas and at IT outsourcing firms. This is less a single enforcement action than the opening move in a wider campaign against employment-based immigration across the industry.
Microsoft has heard versions of this complaint before. Vance said in July 2025 that he didn't "want companies to fire 9,000 American workers and then say we can't find workers here in America," a reference to Microsoft's rolling layoffs over the past year. Microsoft has pushed back every time, telling reporters that "these decisions are based on business need, not visa status," and that H-1B employees were laid off alongside American ones. The company has also said that 78% of the H-1B petitions it filed over a recent 12-month span were extensions for workers already on staff, not new hires brought in from abroad. DOL disclosure data show Microsoft filed 9,492 H-1B labor condition applications in fiscal 2024, with 9,491 certified.
PERM matters because it's the gate between a temporary H-1B visa and a green card. A worker can hold H-1B status for years. But without an approved PERM labor certification, the employer sponsoring them toward permanent residency, that worker's future in the country stays conditional on the employer's goodwill and the visa's renewal cycle. Federal rules already require employers to show they considered laid-off US workers for a role before filing a PERM application tied to it. That's exactly the kind of conflict Microsoft's layoffs created. Google ran into the same friction earlier and paused its own PERM filings to make sure it was complying with Labor Department rules before Microsoft's suspension became public.
The First Circuit rejected the Trump administration's request to reinstate a $100,000 H-1B visa fee on July 24, 2026, keeping the charge blocked while a conflicting D.C. court ruling sets up a likely Supreme Court fight over presidential tax authority. - appeals court blocks H-1B visa fee - H-1B visa fee Supreme Court case
Frankly, the timing says as much as the substance. Microsoft, along with the rest of Big Tech, is in the middle of an AI hiring race that depends heavily on specialized engineering talent, a lot of it recruited globally. A PERM suspension doesn't stop Microsoft from employing H-1B engineers today. But it does freeze their path to a green card, which makes those roles less attractive to the exact workers Microsoft is competing with Google, Meta and Amazon to keep. The company can still pay competitively, but it can no longer offer the same certainty about a worker's long-term status in the US. If rivals aren't hit with the same suspension, that's enough: Microsoft's AI talent pipeline gets measurably harder to hold onto.
That's the real stakes here, and it's bigger than one company's payroll. The H-1B program has been a flashpoint all year. The administration imposed a $100,000 payment requirement for certain new H-1B petitions in September 2025, renewed it in September 2026, and is still fighting in court over whether it can collect it. Vance has repeatedly called the program "completely broken." A green-card suspension aimed at Microsoft, specifically, without public evidence of what the company did wrong, sets a precedent other tech employers now have to worry about. If PERM access can be pulled from a company this size over unspecified fraud allegations tied to its layoffs, any firm that has cut US jobs while sponsoring visas is exposed to the same treatment.
Microsoft hasn't yet issued a direct response to the suspension itself. Given its past posture, defending the legality of its hiring while rejecting any link between layoffs and visa use, a denial is likely to follow. What's missing so far, from both sides, is anything close to a documented account of what actually happened. Vance made an accusation. Microsoft has a defense on record for a related but different complaint. The specific fraud claim behind Thursday's suspension remains unproven in public.

sources.news_title: The Trump administration just cut Microsoft and Adobe off from the green-card pipeline
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Trump administration on Thursday suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six major information-technology outsourcing firms from the federal program that lets employers sponsor skilled foreign workers for permanent residency, accusing the companies of using temporary visas and green-card filings to displace American employees.
Vice President JD Vance, who chairs an administration anti-fraud task force, said the Labor Department will not accept new applications or process pending ones under the Permanent Labor Certification program, known as PERM, for Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. Existing H-1B visas are not canceled. The freeze applies to the labor-certification step that most employers must clear before petitioning for employment-based green cards.
“Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a White House briefing.
He singled out the Redmond, Washington-based company, saying it laid off about 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from roughly 6,300 H-1B approvals and nearly 3,000 green-card filings.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” he said.
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said Microsoft and Adobe, including six outsourcing companies, were suspended because of multiple active federal investigations. Since 2009, he said, the eight companies together have requested almost 3 million foreign workers, received more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and obtained more than 100,000 permanent labor certifications.
“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.
Microsoft and Adobe have yet to release a statement regarding Thursday’s announcement.
An H-1B lets a company employ a foreign worker in a specialty occupation for a limited period, generally up to six years. PERM is the Department of Labor’s finding that no qualified, willing and available U.S. worker can fill the job — a prerequisite for most employer-sponsored green cards.
The Department of Labor’s move lands hardest in the Seattle area. Microsoft’s headquarters and largest U.S. workforce are in Redmond; Adobe maintains a substantial engineering presence in the region. Both firms have long ranked among the heavier users of employment-based visas. Cutting off the green-card pipeline does not force current H-1B employees to leave, but it freezes their path to permanent status through these employers and raises the cost of retaining them if competitors can still sponsor.
Thursday’s action continues a broader second-term effort by the Trump administration to raise the price and narrow the use of skilled-worker visas.
In September 2025 the White House imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B entries from abroad. Lottery registrations at several large IT firms fell sharply the following cycle — by more than 90% at some outsourcing companies, according to Department of Homeland Security data reported by Bloomberg Law.
Federal judges in Massachusetts and California later blocked the fee, ruling the administration lacked authority to impose what amounted to a tax without congressional approval or proper rulemaking; a second injunction in late September 2026 covered a one-year extension of the proclamation.
DHS on Wednesday has separately proposed a fee of roughly $103,000 through formal rulemaking, a step that remains subject to challenge. The Trump administration has also scrutinized optional practical training for foreign graduates and, on Thursday, said they had opened inquiries into nine universities — including Harvard, Yale, Stanford and MIT — over alleged misuse of J-1 exchange visas.
Author: Mario Lotmore

sources.news_title: US Suspends Major Indian IT Firms from Green Card Program
sources.text:
The United States has suspended major Indian IT companies, including Infosys, Wipro, and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), from a programme that facilitates foreign workers’ access to green cards. This suspension is part of an ongoing review by US authorities seeking to ensure compliance with immigration laws related to the employment of foreign nationals.
Impact on Indian IT Companies
This suspension could significantly affect the operational capabilities of the impacted firms as they rely heavily on skilled foreign workers to meet client demands. The rejection from such programmes may hinder their ability to retain talent in the US market, directly influencing their service delivery and growth prospects.
Many of these companies have built substantial operations in the United States, employing thousands of workers. The inability to sponsor green cards may lead to higher turnover rates among staff and difficulty in attracting top talent, as foreign professionals often seek long-term employment stability.
Furthermore, the decision impacts strategic planning within these organisations. The need to rethink hiring and talent acquisition strategies could arise, with companies possibly looking towards more domestic hiring solutions or exploring alternative markets for growth.
Government Response to the Suspension
The US administration has not yet provided detailed reasons behind the suspension, stating that it is part of broader efforts to ensure that foreign labour does not adversely affect American workers. Officials indicate that they are reassessing the rules and regulations surrounding foreign labour to bolster the job market for domestic workers.
While some industry representatives have expressed concern over the implications of this decision, government sources insist that measures are being taken to protect American jobs. The administration is reportedly planning to implement stricter oversight measures for companies that extensively rely on foreign talent.
Consequently, this move may prompt a dialogue between US authorities and Indian IT firms, which could potentially lead to new regulations that affect how these organisations operate in the future. The long-term consequences remain to be seen as the situation develops.
Future Prospects for Affected Firms
As the suspension unfolds, affected firms will need to adapt to the shifting landscape of US immigration policy. The challenge will be for these companies to maintain their competitive edge while complying with new regulations and restrictions. Strategic adjustments in their workforce composition and recruitment processes may become essential.
Furthermore, the outcome of this situation could lead to increased collaboration between Indian IT firms and US authorities. There may be opportunities for dialogue and negotiation that could enable these companies to regain eligibility for the programme in the future, provided that they align with regulatory expectations.
In parallel, companies might seek to enhance their engagement with local universities and educational institutions to develop a home-grown talent pool. This could serve as a proactive strategy to mitigate the challenges associated with dependence on foreign workers.

sources.news_title: US suspends green card route for 8 tech firms
sources.text:
Washington, Oct 8 (SocialNews.XYZ) The Trump administration on Thursday announced the suspension of a key employment-based green card process for eight major technology and outsourcing companies, including India's Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL, as Vice President JD Vance launched a sweeping crackdown on alleged visa fraud.
The action also covers Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. It prevents the companies from filing new permanent labour certification applications and halts the processing of pending applications under the programme.
US Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the decision at a press conference led by Vance, saying the action followed ongoing criminal and federal investigations.
"Due to ongoing criminal investigations led by the Department of Labour's Inspector General Anthony DiEsposito, who will get into this shortly, I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," Sonderling said.
He added that Microsoft and Adobe were also being suspended because of multiple active federal investigations.
"We will not accept or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies," he said.
The Permanent Labour Certification programme, commonly known as PERM, is a crucial step for many employers seeking employment-based permanent residence for foreign workers.
Sonderling said the companies named in the action had collectively requested nearly three million foreign workers since 2009. They had received more than 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications, according to figures he presented.
The administration did not release company-specific findings or details of the alleged violations during the press conference.
Vance accused employers of using the H-1B programme to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign employees.
"The H-1B visa program is meant to allow companies to bring in really the best of the best from outside the United States of America for positions that are completely impossible to fill with American workers," he said.
He singled out Microsoft, alleging that the company had laid off 6,000 American workers while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.
Vance said the administration wanted companies to change their hiring practices rather than leave the American market.
Asked whether the suspension was temporary or permanent, he said, "The suspension of PERM is gonna last as long as it needs to."
He added that the administration had tools to continue the suspension indefinitely but wanted companies to improve their behaviour.
The Justice Department also announced that it was actively investigating companies suspected of favouring foreign workers over Americans.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said criminal prosecutions and civil lawsuits were among the possible enforcement measures.
The announcement could have significant implications for Indian technology professionals and outsourcing companies operating in the United States.
Indian IT companies have long relied on employment-based visa programmes to deploy skilled professionals to American clients. The H-1B programme permits temporary employment in qualifying specialised occupations, while permanent labour certification is part of a separate process through which employers may sponsor workers for permanent residence.
The suspension announced Thursday concerns permanent labour certification applications involving the named companies. It does not, by itself, establish the cancellation of existing H-1B visas or green cards.

sources.news_title: Microsoft Green Card Suspension: Vance Cites Visa Abuse
sources.text:
The Trump administration announced a Microsoft green card suspension Thursday, cutting the tech giant off from the program it uses to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency in the United States.
Vice President JD Vance made the announcement at a White House Fraud Task Force press conference inside the Eisenhower Executive Office Building. He was joined by Stephen Miller, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito and Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson. Along with Microsoft, the Labor Department suspended Adobe and six of the largest IT outsourcing companies in the world: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.
Vance singled out Microsoft. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” he said. He claimed the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.
Here is how the system works. An H-1B is a temporary work visa that lets American companies hire foreign professionals for specialized jobs, and it is especially common in tech. Many of those workers want to stay in the country permanently, so their employer sponsors them for a green card, which grants permanent residency. The first step in that process is called PERM, a labor certification run by the Labor Department. To get it, a company has to show it tested the job market, could not find a qualified American worker for the position, and will pay the going wage for the role. A suspended company cannot move its workers through that step.
The administration claims companies have been using this pathway to bring in cheaper labor, undercut American wages and replace American employees. Vance said the administration still wants tech companies to grow in the United States. “We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers,” he said. “And so, our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”
Sonderling announced the outsourcing suspensions himself. “I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini, and also, due to multiple active federal investigations, @USDOL is suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the program,” he said. Outsourcing firms supply tech workers to other companies on contract, and several of the firms named are based in India. Wall Street reacted quickly, with Infosys shares falling about 2.2 percent and Cognizant dipping about 0.7 percent.
Thursday’s announcement builds on a crackdown that started last month. On September 8, D’Esposito posted on X that Cognizant’s PERM filings had been suspended, and Cloudera was soon added. He said his office was working with the White House Fraud Task Force on the investigation and warned that “handcuffs await.”
The government has not released the specific allegations against Microsoft or Adobe, and it has not said how long the suspensions will last. It is also unclear what happens to applications already in progress. In the Cognizant case, the suspension froze new filings but reportedly did not cancel approvals the company had already received. Microsoft and Adobe had not publicly responded as of publication, leaving employees who were counting on the Microsoft green card process waiting to see where their cases stand.

U.S. Suspends Microsoft, Adobe From Green-Card Labor Program
Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling cited multiple active federal investigations involving the technology companies. The action also covers six major technology services firms.
The U.S. Department of Labor suspended Microsoft and Adobe from the Permanent Labor Certification program Thursday, blocking new applications as federal scrutiny of foreign-worker hiring intensifies.

The Permanent Labor Certification program is used by employers seeking permanent work-based immigration for foreign employees. The decision adds an immigration-related risk for two major U.S. technology companies and a broader group of large technology services firms.
Sonderling said the companies involved had requested nearly 3 million foreign workers since 2009, received more than 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and obtained more than 100,000 permanent labor certifications. He characterized the totals as representing jobs taken from American workers.
The suspensions come as the Trump administration increases enforcement around immigration and foreign hiring programs ahead of the November midterm elections. New applications from the listed companies are now blocked under the Labor Department’s action.

sources.news_title: "Put Americans First": US Penalises Microsoft, Blocks Green Card Filings for Foreign Workers
sources.text:
In a major enforcement escalation targeting corporate visa practices, the Trump administration on Thursday announced the suspension of tech giant Microsoft from the federal PERM program, effectively blocking the company from applying for permanent residency (green cards) on behalf of its H-1B visa holders.
The action was formally unveiled during a White House press briefing led by US Vice President JD Vance, who accused the Redmond-based technology firm of systemically abusing the US immigration process.
”Replaced American Workers with Foreign Labor”
Justifying the harsh regulatory crackdown, Vice President Vance alleged that Microsoft engaged in fraudulent practices by conducting domestic workforce layoffs while simultaneously filing foreign labor certifications.
Speaking to reporters, Vance delivered a sharp rebuke of the corporate employment model:
”If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. There is no company in the United States that has abused this system more than Microsoft.”
The suspension targets the Department of Labor’s PERM (Program for Electronic Review Management) labor certification pathway, a mandatory preliminary step employers must complete before sponsoring an H-1B visa holder for an employment-based green card.
Broader Industry Impact
The crackdown on Microsoft comes alongside wider enforcement measures targeting major tech conglomerates and academic institutions. Administration officials signalled that companies attempting to leverage foreign visa frameworks to reduce labor costs amid domestic downsizing will face immediate exclusion from immigration sponsorship programs.
Technology firms represent the single largest user base of the H-1B visa category, with foreign professionals from India receiving nearly three-quarters of all annual approvals. The freeze on PERM filings poses significant operational and career uncertainty for thousands of foreign engineers and IT professionals currently employed under Microsoft’s corporate umbrella.
